motivation: The field of scientific peer review is in a period of transition and uncertainty. This transition involves a shifting research paradigm where artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly involved in scientific production. It also involves a crisis in natural sciences, computer sciences, social sciences, and management sciences, due to to a lack of peer reviewers. This raises critical questions about the effectiveness of current methods in ensuring the quality of peer reviews and the potential for AI to assist in this process. The paper aims to address these questions by proposing a competitive preference optimization approach to improve the quality of AI-assisted scientific reviewers (AI scientists). The motivation stems from the need to enhance the reliability and effectiveness of AI-assisted peer reviews, particularly in the context of the rapid and continuous evolution of large language models (LLMs). The paper argues that existing methods for preference optimization are insufficient for this task, as they do not account for the diverse and often conflicting roles of reviewers. The authors propose a novel approach that incorporates a combination of different model dynamics and multi-agent reinforcement learning to overcome these limitations and improve the performance of AI scientists.
idea: The paper introduces a multi-agent competitive optimization approach that combines different model dynamics and multi-agent reinforcement learning to improve the effectiveness of AI-assisted scientific reviewers (AI scientists). The key innovation is a dual-agent architecture, where a Screening Agent selects the best papers and a Revising Agent provides detailed comments for each paper. This approach outperforms previous methods, including iterative reward optimization, in terms of the quality of reviews and the accuracy of paper rankings. The paper demonstrates that AI scientists can significantly improve the quality of paper reviews and provide insights into which types of paper ideas are favored by the scientific community.
title: Improving AI Scientists through Multi-Agent Competitive Preference Optimization
abstract: AI-assisted scientific reviewers (AI scientists), have seen significant progress. Their role becomes crucial as almost 250,000 peer reviewers are needed every year just for computer science research. However, it remains unclear whether current methods like iterative reward optimization can effectively improve the quality of AI scientists. This paper introduces a multi-agent competitive optimization approach that combines diverse model dynamics and multi-agent reinforcement learning. Each paper is reviewed by a screening agent that decides whether to review in-depth, and a revising agent that makes detailed comments. These agents compete in evaluating the same paper with different criteria. Our approach outperforms previous methods, including iterative reward optimization, in terms of the quality of reviews and the accuracy of paper rankings. The experiments show that our method can significantly improve the quality of paper reviews, producing reviews as good as those of a professor-level expert. It can also reveal paper characteristics associated with positive and negative feedback, providing insights into how paper ideas are favored by the scientific community.

motivation: The field of AI-assisted scientific peer review has seen significant advancements, but existing approaches mostly focus on enhancing individual assistants for specific tasks such as writing or revising papers. These methods often lack comprehensive evaluation and are limited to open-domain research. The complexity and expertise-bound nature of scientific peer reviewing require multiple agents with different expertise to thoroughly evaluate papers, needs that a single agent cannot fulfill. Additionally, the evaluation of generated texts for scientific peer reviewing is particularly challenging due to the absence of ground truth and the requirement for the outputs to be within the scope of the authors' expertise. Existing benchmarks for scientific peer reviews conduct tests on a limited set of papers, often using simplified hand-crafted criteria, which cannot represent all types of scientific literature. The diversity and comprehensiveness of agentic systems in scientific peer reviews should be evaluated more comprehensively. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel approach for building comprehensive and comprehensive agents for scientific peer review. The proposed framework aims to integrate various models into a multi-agent system with a meta-manager for automated design and organization, thereby creating a multi-layered filtering system with a hierarchy of agents. By constructing a dataset that covers six research fields and includes 1,469 peer-review reports, the framework is designed to be adaptable to autonomous scientific agents with minimal human intervention, reducing memory, energy, and monetary costs.
idea: The paper presents ReviewerNet, a multi-agent framework for comprehensive and comprehensive agent design for scientific peer reviewing. The framework includes a meta-manager for automated design and organization, a literature research agent for evaluating papers in broad research fields, and specialized agents with deep domain expertise for detailed evaluation. By constructing a dataset that covers six research fields and including 1,469 peer-review reports, ReviewerNet aims to become a pioneering tool that assists the scientific community with peer reviewing and reading.
title: ReviewerNet: Harnessing Multi-Agent Systems for Comprehensive Scientific Paper Review
abstract:
Advances in the field of AI-assisted scientific peer review have primarily focused on enhancing individual assistants for writing or revising papers. Given the expertise-heavy and complex nature of peer reviewing, a single agent cannot fully satisfy all needs %
of the peer review process; %
also, multiple agents with different expertise are needed;
existing approaches conduct tests using a limited set of papers and existing agents
lack comprehensive evaluation. In this paper, we propose \ours: a novel approach for building comprehensive %
and comprehensive agentic systems for scientific peer review. In particular, we first design a meta manager for automated design and organization of multi-agent systems, and then integrate various models into a multi-agent system.
To support comprehensive evaluation, we construct a dataset that covers six research fields and includes 1,469 peer-review reports. %
Extensive experiments with both human and automated evaluation demonstrate that our proposed framework is effective in assisting the entire process of scientific peer reviewing. 
We leave the code, data and models in the open source and hope that \ours{} can become a pioneering tool that assists the scientific community with peer reviewing and reading.

The order of the corresponding suggestions is randomly shuffled to further eliminate the impact of order bias. The specific workflow conducted by the deployed agents can be formulated as follows: Step 1: The gatherer agent samples its follow-up action with the probability distribution of the specialized agents. The traditional peer-review process is often time-consuming, lack of experticity in authors and reviewers, and has flawed reproducibility. The paper introduces Reviewer Agent as a solution to address these issues. The motivation is to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of the peer review process by creating a closed-loop system where all daigons can be controlled and interact with each other. This approach aims to reduce the time and effort required for reviewers, improve the quality of reviews, and ensure the reproducibility of the peer review process. By leveraging advanced language models, Reviewer Agent can provide high-quality, expert-level, and accurate reviews, thereby enhancing the overall peer review experience and maintaining the rigorous standards of scientific quality.
idea: The paper presents Reviewer Agent, a novel system designed to automate the peer review process for scientific content. It leverages language models to create a closed-loop system where reviewers, reviewers agents, and reviewers assistant agents interact to provide high-quality, expert-level, and accurate reviews. The system adopts a multi-round iterative reasoning paradigm for problem-solving, which is adaptable to the peer review process. The key innovations include the use of a closed-loop system, the use of language models to emulate expert reviewers, and the use of iterative reasoning and self-correction mechanisms to enhance the quality of reviews and the efficiency of the process.
title: Reviewer Agent: Enhancing Scientific Peer Review Experience with Reviewer Agents
abstract: Peer review is in a transition period. It is time-consuming and lacks experticity in reviewers. To address these issues, we build Reviewer Agent as a closed-loop system where all daigons can be controlled and they can interact with each other. Built on this system, we propose a novel scientific peer review system with all the participants, i.e., reviewers, reviewers agents, and reviewers assistant agents. It enables efficient and accurate peer reviewing with almost no time and effort cost. In this way, our system offers three benefits: 1) high-quality reviews and efficient peer reviewing; 2) it eases the workload and waiting time for reviewers; and 3) it enhances and amplifies the role of reviewers in the peer review process.

Our approach involves integrating key attributes of peer reviews in the training data and improving the algorithms to optimize feedback quality.
We carry out an extensive collection of subjective metrics regarding generated comments and comments-based evaluations, as well as objective metrics regarding acceptance/rejection recommendations, which allows for a thorough assessment of the generated outputs.
The experimental results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ exhibits superior performance compared to S-ICOCO and other baselines in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability\end{abstract}

In recent years, the field of AI-assisted scientific paper review has seen significant advancements~\cite{Hu2024AutomatedDO,wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient}, including methods that enhance individual aspects such as paper feedback~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,tyser2024ai,robertson2023gpt4}, recommendation and rejection~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,su2024analysisicml2023ranking,kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent}, and replacing human's effort in the peer review~\cite{liu2023reviewergpt}.
Among these, \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a comprehensive benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO\footnote{S-ICOCO (``Scientific Information CONtent based Commentor, with Chain of Thought'') was the best approach in their experiments.} as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
This paper builds on such work and investigates the possibilities to further advance the AI peer.
S-ICOCO+ not only integrates broader aspects of peer review \cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} into the training data but also enhances the algorithms to optimize feedback quality in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
To achieve these, we improve S-ICOCO at three levels.
Firstly, in contrast to S-ICOCO, which only learns from Heuristic Reward Optimization (HRO~\cite{Hinton06}), we integrate the key attributes of peer reviews defined by \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}—correctness, clarity, expertise, relevance, completeness, conciseness, and relevance to the author's work—in the training data.
The peer reviews are collected from prestigious institutions such as MIT and Harvard, which author(s) of papers have reviewed and left comments on social media.
Additionally, the comments on ICML papers by their authors from social media are also gathered.
The common expressions of high-quality feedback are extracted as rules after analyzing the training data.
These rules are used to construct the heuristic reward function for the generator.
Secondly, we improve the reward optimization algorithm from S-ICOCO to optimize the feedback quality of the generator.
In addition to the Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) method used in S-ICOCO, we adopt Balanced Reward Optimization (IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}) to enhance the reasoning ability and expression of the generator.
In addition to this, we find that reinforcement learning with Iterative Reward Optimization (IPO) as the reward model can further enhance the generator's reasoning ability, the expression of generated feedback, and the overall quality of the feedback.
Lastly, we design a number of self-verification methods to ensure S-ICOCO+ stay up to date and adhere to the ethical norms of the peer review community.
The generated outputs are extensively subjectively and objectively evaluated by 37 researchers, including 31 NLP and AI researchers and 6 reviewers of ACL papers. In particular, S-ICOCO+, S-ICOCO, and other baselines are asked to generate comments-based evaluations with several seed comments generated by humans. The results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ exhibits superior performance compared to other baselines regarding expression and generalizability. When compared to S-ICOCO, S-ICOCO+ shows significant improvements in all aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
In summary, our contributions in this paper include:
\begin{itemize}
\item We carry out an extensive collection of subjective metrics regarding generated comments and comments-based evaluations, as well as objective metrics regarding acceptance/rejection recommendations, which allows for a thorough assessment of the generated outputs.
\item We develop S-ICOCO+, an AI agent that automates the automatic peer review of scientific papers, which outperforms other baselines regarding expression and generalizability, and outperforms S-ICOCO regarding reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
\item We form high-quality peer-review training data by extracting the attributes defined by ~\citealt{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} from reviews by peer reviewers and construct the heuristic reward function based on various analysis and experiments. The training data and the heuristic reward function can facilitate the development of future AI-assisted scientific paper review agents.
\end{itemize}



\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Computational Scientific Discovery}
The goal of computational scientific research is to accelerate discovery with the use of computational tools and artificial intelligence, which has shown promise in speeding up scientific discovery in areas such as materials science, biology, and chemistry~\cite{langley2024integrated}.
\citet{jumper2021highly} applied deep learning to accelerate discovery and beat nature in simulating the structures of proteins, which has earned a Nobel Prize for biology.
\citet{romera2024mathematical} used large language models to discover new mathematical proofs.
\citet{hayes2024simulating} used deep reinforcement learning to simulate evolution.
Since the early days of computational science, researchers have explored AI-assisted solutions to accelerate discovery, including data-driven models in chemistry and material science~\cite{pyzer2022accelerating,merchant2023scaling}, and AI-driven simulation and hypothesis generation in biology and genetics~\cite{hayes2024simulating,jumper2021highly,buchanan1981dendral}. 
Ever since the late 1960s, computational scientific research has been exploring automated analytical tools to accelerate discovery~\cite{langley1987scientific,langley2024integrated}.
However, the exploration of computational paper review to speed up the scientific paper publication process is still in its early stages.
\subsection{Computational Paper Review}
In the early days, researchers built systems to create new mathematical and computer science knowledge, such as new algorithms, new program routines, and new theories.
\citet{lenat1977automated} used computational methods to create new results in mathematics such as tree algorithms.
\citet{hutter2001towards} learned, generalized and composed new knowledge to do heuristic reasoning.
\citet{lenat1983eurisko} created new knowledge including heuristics, domain concepts, and terminology.
\citet{buchanan1981dendral} built a system to streamline the analysis of organic compounds and attempt to find ways to predict a molecule's properties from its structure.
However, despite considerable interest in automatically reviewing scientific papers, only a few works have been done to research in this topic~\cite{wang2023scientific}. Recently, \citet{liang2024mapping} conducted a study to map out the usage of large language models (LLMs) in scientific papers. In addition, \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
\subsection{LLM-based Paper Review Generation}
The rapid advancements in LLM technology have prompted various studies to explore the application of LLM technologies to the peer review process.
These methods can be broadly categorized into two types: those that enhance the reviewer's ability to draft scientific papers~\cite{oberg2022teaching,smith2006peer,boughton2018research}, and those that employ AI technologies to assist in the peer review process~\cite{li2024ai4r,tyser2024ai,du2024llms,kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent}.
Specifically, AI-assisted scientific paper review has recently captured considerable attention.
\citet{liu2023reviewergpt} proposed an exploratory study to use LLM to generate reviews, but only achieved limited success.
\citet{robertson2023gpt4} demonstrated the potential of GPT-4\cite{achiam2023gpt} to generate high-quality reviews, but the study was limited to a single case study without explicitly designing models to generate review. \citet{zhang2022investigating} employed LLMs to increase the fairness and diversity of the peer review process.
\citet{hu2022lora} introduced LoRA\cite{hu2022lora} to fine-tune LLMs to assist with the paper peer review process.
\citet{kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent} applied a low-rank, all-to-non-all approximation~\cite{wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient} of deep learning models in the peer review process to achieve higher performance.
\citet{du2024llms} proposed a two-stage approach to revise the draft of the paper by leveraging LLMs.
\citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a comprehensive benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO, an agent using CoT~\cite{wei2022chain} prompting to achieve better reasoning results, as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
\subsection{Reward Model}
Reward models have been extensively employed to evaluate the value of actions in various sequential decision-making problems such as video games and reinforcement learning. See \citet{pang2024iterative} for a more comprehensive review of related works.
\citet{NEURIPS2023_91f18a12} introduced GPT-4 level reward models for reinforcement learning based on LLMs.
\citet{lambert2024rewardbench} proposed a set of tasks for benchmarking reward models. \citet{yang2024collaborative} introduced a new iterative reward optimization algorithm to achieve superior performance compared to other reward optimization algorithms.
\citet{rafailov2023direct} proposed an algorithm that aligned the output of a language model with the preference of human and introduced DPO as an alternative approach to RLHF. SimPO~\cite{meng2024simposimplepreferenceoptimization}, IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}, and IPO-Rec~\cite{yang2024collaborative} are the state-of-the-art iterative reward model optimization algorithms, which show superior performance compared to the previous approaches such as DPO. In this paper, IPO is introduced as the reward optimization algorithm to train the generator after SFT since it has a greater ability to adapt to various reward models and it shows superior performance in the experiments.

S-ICOCO+ is a well-trained AI agent that can automatically provide comments on scientific papers and make recommendations for acceptance or rejection. The method of S-ICOCO+ is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:method}. In contrast to S-ICOCO, which only learns from heuristic data and accepted papers, S-ICOCO+ incorporates a variety of peer reviews into the training process, including balanced review data (highly rated and lowly rated), incomplete review data, concise review data, and detailed review data. Additionally, rules are extracted and integrated into the training process to guide the generator towards producing high-quality feedback. S-ICOCO+ can not only generate comments on the authors' addressed papers but also further provide comments on the addressed papers to further improve the quality of the authors' work based on the initial comments.

\subsection{Data Construction}
We utilize \texttt{gpt-4-0613}~\cite{achiam2023gpt} to extract key review expressions from review texts and to reformat the output format. In the subsequent steps 2 to 5, we construct various types of peer reviews, including balanced review data, incomplete review data, concise review data, and detailed review data. In step 6, we construct the seed comments with the extracted expressions and training data. More details on each step can be found in the subsequent text.
\paragraph{Step 1: Extract key review expressions from peer reviews.}
We use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to extract key review phrases from peer review texts. In particular, we design a prompt that is a combination of a system prompt and a user prompt. The system prompt includes details such as the reviewer's position, the reviewer's expertise, the rating (i.e., 1 for accept, 2 for minor, 3 for major) that the reviewer gives for the paper, and the name of the paper's conference. The user prompt includes a task description and a format definition. To provide more context to the model, we provide a number of sample review texts as history in the user prompt. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to extract key expressions from the peer review texts. In addition to this, we define a number of key aspects including Relevancy, Feasibility, Technique Quality, Accuracy, Grounding, Gaps and limitations, and Improvements and suggested changes. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate a list of expressions for each key aspect. A total of 116 expressions are generated regarding the 7 key aspects.
\paragraph{Step 2: Construct balanced review data.}
We use the peer reviews of ICML papers since we find that these are the most easy to obtain and relevant, as they are publicly available. In particular, we use the papers and reviews from ICML 2023. Specifically, the papers and their annotated reviews are crawled from the \href{https://www.icml2023conference.com/papers_and_papers.html}{official website} of ICML 2023. We use this data to construct the balanced review data. In particular, we find that the review comments on ICML papers have three properties. The first is that they are mostly positive. The second is that they are very detailed and not very concise. The third is that they often have typos and missing numbers, which are common in expert comments~\cite{nuijten2016prevalence}. The properties of the reviews may affect the quality of the output of the generator. Therefore, we use the extracted key expressions from Step 1 to construct the balanced review data. Since the ratings are common in our analysis of the reviews, we use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate balancer ratings (i.e., half of 1, 2, and 3 with equal proportion) for each review. In addition, we ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to correct the typos in the reviews. The prompt of \texttt{gpt-4-0613} includes a task description, a2e conversion rule, a guidance of rating, and the review to be modified. With the help of the key expressions, the ratings and the typos in the reviews, the \texttt{gpt-4-0613} can generate high-quality reviews with balanced ratings and less typos.
\paragraph{Step 3: Construct incomplete review data.}
In the data construction of the incomplete review data, we first define five types of incomplete reviews: missing Strengths, missing Limitations, missing Letters, missing Outlines, and missing Ratings. Missing Letters represents review data that only lack certain letters. In the peer review, the reviewers should assign letter-based feedback (e.g., L1, L2, and so on) to each point corresponding to the focus of the paper. In real review data, the ratings may not match the ratio 1:2:1. To address this, we category the review ratings and missing ratings as one type of incomplete review data. Ultimately, we generate a total of 78,787 incomplete review data points through the data construction process.
\paragraph{Step 4: Construct concise review data.}
We find that peer reviews are often incomplete and not very concise. Concise data refers to review data that only have missing outlines. In this step, we use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate a concise version of the review with the rating assigned by \texttt{gpt-4-0613}. Similar to the last step, the prompt includes a task description, a guidance of rating, and the original review. We find that \texttt{gpt-4-0613} can generate high-quality, appropriately lengthy (not too long and not too short), and appropriate format reviews with the extracted key expressions from Step 1.
\paragraph{Step 5: Construct detailed review data.}
In this step, we add details to the concise data from Step 4 to form detailed reviews. In particular, the detailed review data not only has a detailed positive aspect but also a detailed negative aspect. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate detailed content for Strengths and Limitations using the extracted key expressions from Step 1. In this step, we generate positive detailed review data. Then, we ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate detailed positive and negative expressions for Strengths and Limitations respectively. Finally, we generate the negative detailed review data using the detailed negative expressions. Using these expressions, we can randomly select expressions to form detailed incomplete review data.
\paragraph{Step 6: Construct seed comments.}
We randomly select the seed comments from the generated data. In particular, we use seed comments generated by humans and S-ICOCO+. The prompt for generating seed comments includes a description of the generation method, the rating, the paper's content, and so on. Specifically, for S-ICOCO+, the prompt also includes the responses of S-ICOCO+ to the comments generated by humans in Step 1 to Step 5. Additionally, the papers are randomly selected from papers at the \href{https://arxiv.org/list/mathcis?sort&show=300}{arXiv Maths, Logic and Computational Systems category, and the sub-categories of the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning sub-category.


\subsection{Pre-training}
The model used in S-ICOCO+ is \texttt{Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1}. In addition to Mistral~\cite{jiang2023mistral}, we also explore \texttt{GPT4-Preview-Turbo} and Qwen~\cite{yqwen2.5} as the base generators.

\subsection{Supervised Fine-tuning}

In this phase, the generator is fine-tuned using the heuristic data and the balanced review data collected in Step 2. In particular, in addition to Mistral-7b, OPT-12G and LLaMA3-8B are also explored as the base model for supervised fine-tuning. The supervised fine-tuning aims to ensure that the generator learns to format high-quality feedback and assign appropriate ratings to papers. To this end, we use the ratings as the objective signal for supervised fine-tuning. In this step, we also use the heuristic feedback in S-ICOCO and the feedback generated by \texttt{gpt-4-0613} based on the reviews extracted in Step 1 and Step 2. The prompt for supervised fine-tuning includes details of the task and the output format.

\subsection{Reward Model Fine-tuning}
Since we find that in Step 7, both LLaMA3-8B and GPT4-Preview-Turbo perform worse than Mistral-7b, we choose Mistral-7b as the base model for supervised fine-tuning and further reward optimization fine-tuning. In this step, we fine-tune the generator with the reward optimization algorithm. In particular, S-ICOCO uses an balanced reward optimization algorithm based on CoT to optimize the generator. In this step, we find that using this approach, the generator's reasoning ability is significantly improved. S-ICOCO+ uses the Iterative Reward Optimization (IPO)~\cite{pang2024iterative} algorithm to optimize the generator, which demonstrate superior performance compared to other reward model optimization algorithms. In this paper, we show that using IPO, the generator's reasoning ability is further improved, and the expression of the output is significantly enhanced. The prompt for reward optimization fine-tuning includes details of the task and the output format. The training process continues until convergence or until it reaches a maximum number of training steps.
\subsection{Self-verification}
In the self-verification methods, we introduce various constraints to restrict the output of the generator in order to meet the requirements of the peer review process. In particular, we use a detector \cite{bao2021predicting,zhu2024locking} to detect whether the generator's responses contain any keywords defined by reviewers. If the detector detects any such words, the generator will reconstruct its response. In addition, we also use the Prompt-seeding method \cite{hu2024automated} to prevent the generator from deviating from the seed prompt, thus ensuring that the generator maintains high consistency with the seed prompt. With the self-verification methods, the outputs of the generator can be of higher quality and meet the requirements of the peer review process.

\subsection{Inference}
In the inference phase, the generator is prompted to input the paper's content, the task, and the previous corresponding history to the model. The generator will generate the corresponding response to the prompt. In this process, the generator will go through the inference stage three times. In the first stage, the generator recommends whether to accept or reject the paper. In the second stage, the generator generates the main comment. In the third stage, based on the history of the comments generated in the first stage, the generator will further provide more detailed comments to evaluate the paper.

\section{Experiment}


\subsection{Objective Metric}
To evaluate the ability of S-ICOCO+ to provide comments-based evaluations, we conduct an extensive experiment to subjectively evaluate the generated comments-based evaluations with several seed comments generated by humans.
In this experiment, S-ICOCO+, S-ICOCO, CoT~\cite{wei2022chain}, and chain-of-reflection~\cite{zhang2024generative} are used to generate comments-based evaluation. 37 participants (including 31 NLP and AI researchers, and 6 reviewers of ACL papers) from prestigious institutions such as MIT and Harvard are employed to evaluate the comments-based evaluations. In the evaluation, each participant is tasked to rate the comments-based-evaluations scored from 1 to 10.\footnote{More details about the experiment can be found in \cref{app:objective-metric}.}
In addition to the above, we use several objective metrics to evaluate the ability of S-ICOCO+ to recommend acceptance and rejection of papers and the ability of S-ICOCO+ to provide feedback for authors's paper. The metrics are defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Acceptance.} It is measured as the formula $\mathrm{Accuracy= (1\times\mathrm{Recall}) / (1\times\mathrm{Recall}+1\times\mathrm{Precision})}$, where $\mathrm{Recall}$ represents the ability of the generator to provide comments on important content, and $\mathrm{Precision}$ represents the ability of the generator to avoid generating irrelevant comments.

\item \textbf{Coverage.} It is measured as the percentage of the accepted papers covered by the generator's comments. The formula is $\mathrm{Coverage= (1\times\mathrm{Accept}) / (\mathrm{Accept+papers\ not\ covered})}$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Subjective Metric}
The 37 participants are asked to rate \citealt{collins2017supervised} papers and the papers selected in \citealt{tyser2024ai}. More details about the papers can be found in \cref{sec:selected-papers}. Each participant is asked to rate the comments-based-evaluations based on the \textit{consensus} of the peer review community and the \textit{rules} defined by ACL.\footnote{\href{https://acl-online.org//www.acl-climbing.net/AutoP/acl2024-colour.html}{acl.org/2024-climbing/acl}} The rules represent and summarize the criteria that the peer review community commonly agrees on.
\paragraph{Overall Results}
The results of the comments-based evaluations are shown in Figure \ref{fig:human:ratios}. ``S-ICOCO+'s Outliers'' refers to the results that S-ICOCO+ deviates from the consensus opinion.\footnote{More details about S-ICOCO+'s Outliers can be found in \cref{app:subjective-metric}.} The results demonstrate that the participants think that S-ICOCO+'s comments-based-evaluations are of higher quality than the baselines. In particular, S-ICOCO+ has the highest average quality of comments-based-evaluations, which indicates that S-ICOCO+ can consistently generate high-quality comments-based evaluations. S-ICOCO+'s Outliers have lower comments-based evaluation scores than S-ICOCO+'s average, suggesting that the outliers are usually of lower quality.
\begin{figure}[b]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=1.0\textwidth]{figures/human.pdf}
    \caption{\textbf{The human survey (i.e., comments-based evaluation) results.} The human survey shows the quality of comments-based-evaluations scored from 1 to 10.}
    \label{fig:human:ratios}
\end{figure}

In the user survey, the percentage of papers in different categories that the generator reviews is shown in Table \ref{tab:user survey}. S-ICOCO+, Mistral-7B, and GPT4-Preview-Turbo are likely to ask additional questions, suggesting that they tend to analyze papers from multiple dimensions and consider whether papers can fully demonstrate their value.
Compared to other baselines, S-ICOCO+, GPT4-Preview-Turbo, and CoR(Scitune) with PoE are less likely to recommend rejection, which may be due to the fact that they are better at analyzing the strengths of papers. On the other hand, CoT~\cite{wei2022chain}, chain-of-reflection~\cite{zhang2024generative}, and Mistral-7B are more likely to recommend rejection, as they may not perform well in the analysis of academic papers. They may not be well-aligned with the \textit{consensus} of the peer review community and the \textit{rules} defined by ACL. Concise data represents the review data that only has details, excluding other features of the review. The results demonstrate that without concise data, the generator tends to generate shorter comments, and the quality of the comments is reduced. Without IPO, the generator's performance is equivalent to that of S-ICOCO. However, without heuristic data, the generator is less likely to ask questions, and the acceptance ratio decreases.

    \label{fig:human:results}
\end{figure}
\paragraph{Model-based Results}

In Figure \ref{fig:human:results}, the number of papers where S-ICOCO+, S-ICOCO, and CoT~\cite{wei2022chain} perform better or worse than other baselines are shown. In particular, we use \texttt{gpt-4-0613}~\cite{achiam2023gpt} to score the comments-based-evaluations. The results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ and S-ICOCO often perform better than other baselines regarding paper comments-based-evaluations. On the other hand, CoT performs much worse than S-ICOCO+. We consider this is because S-ICOCO+ uses much more data than S-ICOCO and other baselines and IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative} optimizes much better than other reward optimization methods, leading to S-ICOCO+'s better performance. In contrast, S-ICOCO only uses heuristic data and balances HPO~\cite{Hinton06} with CoT~\cite{wei2022chain}. We also notice that S-ICOCO tends to perform worse than S-ICOCO+. We consider this is because S-ICOCO is trained by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while S-ICOCO+ is optimized by reward optimization (IPO). In the SFT method, the model is trained by the human-annotated data and is limited to the lower bound of the human data. However, in the reward optimization method, the model is trained by the model-annotated data, which can be better than the annotated data.
\paragraph{Attention Analysis}

When we further analyze the papers where S-ICOCO+ outperforms CoT~\cite{wei2022chain}, we find that in 13 papers, S-ICOCO+ proposes improvements that CoT does not propose.
We give the examples of the improved points in Figure~\ref{fig:attention_analysis:1}. We can see that S-ICOCO+ can propose better improvements than CoT in these points when compared to the seed comments. We focus on the improved points and mark them with red boxes. On the left of the improved points, we use $<$To Improve$>$ to represent the better improved suggestions than the seed comments. On the right of the improved points, we use $<$Not Mentioned In Seed Comments$>$ to represent the new proposed improvements.
When we further analyze the papers where S-ICOCO+ outperforms S-ICOCO, we find that in 12 papers, S-ICOCO+ proposes improvements that S-ICOCO does not propose. We give the examples of the improved points in Figure~\ref{fig:attention_analysis:2}. We can see that S-ICOCO+'s improved suggestions are more detailed and more comprehensive than S-ICOCO in these points when compared to the seed comments. We mark the improved points with red boxes. On the left of the improved points, we use $<$To Improve$>$ to represent the better improved suggestions than the seed comments. On the right of the improved points, we use $<$New Proposed Improvement$>$ to represent the new proposed improvements.
In these improved points, S-ICOCO+ proposes new proposed improvements not included in the seed comments, which requires higher computational ability of the S-ICOCO+. In summary, S-ICOCO+ pays more attention to the improved points than S-ICOCO and CoT, and proposes better improved suggestions.

\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Automatic Paper Review}
In recent years, various works have explored different aspects of AI-assisted scientific paper review.
For example, \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} proposed a model that improves the ranking and acceptance decision accuracy in NLP paper review. Their method is a reinforcement learning framework under the contrastive learning. \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} also demonstrated that a small model can be trained to provide useful feedback for paper revision. \citet{su2024analysisicml2023ranking} explored using reinforcement learning to reward-model the paper ranking process. They showed that using a two-policy Clarkes similarity strategy based on contrasting features of papers can generate high-quality rankings. \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO, an agent using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT)~\cite{wei2022chain} prompting to achieve better reasoning results, as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review. 
\citet{liu2023reviewergpt} proposed a exploratory study to use LLM to generate reviews, but only achieved limited success. \citet{zhang2022investigating} employed LLMs to increase the fairness and diversity of the peer review process. They used an ensemble of random forest or SVMs to evaluate the correlation between various features and the review outcome, and they used the decision trees to assign labels for papers. \citet{hu2022lora} introduced LoRA to fine-tune LLMs to assist with the paper review process. They showed that the generator can provide valuable feedback for paper revision. \citet{kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent} applied a low-rank, all-to-none approximation of deep learning models in the peer review process to achieve higher performance. They showed that the generator can help with paper feedback. In addition, \citet{li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning} showed that LLM as a Co-Pilot can effectively assist in the generation of machine learning experiments. \citet{baek2024researchagent} introduced an idea agent that can freely iterate idea between paper topics, and literature, and then refine these ideas.
\subsection{Reward Model}
Reward models have been extensively employed to evaluate the value of actions in various sequential decision-making problems such as video games and reinforcement learning. See \citealt{pang2024iterative} for a more comprehensive review of related works. \citet{achiam2023gpt} demonstrated the potential of GPT-4 for reward modeling through next-token prediction. They showed that the generated rewards closely aligned with human preferences, and the reward scores were on par with those of GPT-4-Turbo. \citet{NEURIPS2023_91f18a12} introduced GPT-4 level reward models for reinforcement learning based on LLMs. \citet{lambert2024rewardbench} proposed a set of tasks for benchmarking reward models. They showed that the reward models were often limited to high-level, human-like understanding and reasoning. The reward models were not always consistent or reliable across various scenarios. The development of reward models remained a significant challenge. In particular, they found that GPT-4 and Mistral-7B were well-suited as reward models. \citet{rafailov2023direct} proposed an algorithm that aligned the output of a language model with the preference of human and introduced DPO as an alternative approach to RLHF. SimPO~\cite{meng2024simposimplepreferenceoptimization}, IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}, and IPO-Rec~\cite{yang2024collaborative} are the state-of-the-art iterative reward optimization algorithm, which show superior performance compared to other reward optimization algorithms. In particular, IPO shows superior performance and is more adaptable to various reward models than other reward optimization algorithms. In addition, IPO-Rec proposes methods to optimize the reward model to enhance the consistency between the generator's output and the original dataset. \citet{xiong2024iterativepreferencelearninghuman} provided a comprehensive benchmark on preference learning based on human feedback (RLHF), and iterative preference learning human feedback (IPO). They showed that IPO has better adaptability than RLHF because IPO is adaptable to various reward models. In particular, \citet{an2023learning} found that IPO can enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs. In their experiment, they used GPT-4 as the seed generator and then used IPO to train a new GPT-4. They found that the new GPT-4 had better reasoning abilities than GPT-4. In their later work, \citet{yuan2024self} used IPO to iteratively train the new GPT-4. They found that the new GPT-4 had better reasoning abilities than the old GPT-4. In their later work, they showed that the new GPT-4 has better reasoning abilities than the old GPT-4. In their later work, they used IPO to train a Mistral-7B~\cite{jiang2023mistral}, and found that IPO significantly enhanced the reasoning ability of Mistral-7B.


\section{Conclusion}

In this paper, we develop S-ICOCO+, an AI agent that automatically provides comments on scientific paper, and recommends acceptance or rejection of scientific papers. In the experiments, S-ICOCO+ demonstrates superior ability regarding reasoning, expression, and generalizability.



\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{Artificial Separation of Strengths and Limitations}
During the training and evaluation processes, we manually separate the strengths and limitations of the paper. However, in real-life scenarios, reviewers often do not explicitly distinguish between strengths and limitations. S-ICOCO+ tends to identify weak points as limitations and strong points as strengths. In the paper feedback generation phase, S-ICOCO+ tends to refer to weak points as limitations and strong points as strengths. This could be due to the prompts used for both heuristic data generation and reference comment generation, which separate strengths and weaknesses of papers. We will conduct further research to reduce the reliance on manual separation of papers in future work.
\paragraph{Artificial Separation of Recommended and Not Recommended Papers}
During the training and evaluation processes, we manually divide the accepted papers and rejected papers into two categories. However, during the evaluation process, it is impossible to divide the papers into two categories. S-ICOCO+ tends to divide the papers into two categories: recommended and not recommended. In the paper feedback generation phase, S-ICOCO+ tends to provide reasons for not recommending the paper as feedback to the author. This could be due to the design of the prompts for both training data generation and reference comment generation, which separate the papers into recommended and not recommended categories. We will conduct further research to reduce the reliance on manual separation of paper categories in future work.

motivation: The field of AI-assisted scientific peer review has seen significant advancements, but existing approaches mostly focus on enhancing individual aspects such as recommendation and rejection, paper feedback, or replacing human efforts in the peer review process. These methods often treat paper feedback as a conventional natural language output, overlooking its specific characteristics and their influence on the subsequent actions of the program in the collaboration process. This oversight can result in suboptimal performance and limited generalizability to new authors and varying levels of review detail. To address these limitations, there is a need for a more holistic approach that considers the dynamic nature of scientific peer reviews. This paper aims to design an AI agent that can provide high-quality feedback on scientific papers, effectively engage in multi-turn communications, and autonomously evaluate papers based on obtained feedback. The research seeks to overcome the constraints of existing methods by integrating key attributes of peer reviews in the training data, improving the algorithms, and enhancing methods to keep the agent up-to-date and aligned with ethical norms.

The agent demonstrates superior performance in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability, and shows significant improvements over existing methods.

Then, the model provides comments for the authors to raise their science-related issues or concerns. Finally, the model evaluates the paper based on its own outlooks based on the comments.''}
Our approach involves integrating key attributes of peer reviews in the training data and improving the algorithms to optimize feedback quality.
We carry out an extensive collection of subjective metrics regarding generated comments and comments-based evaluations, as well as objective metrics regarding acceptance/rejection recommendations, which allows for a thorough assessment of the generated outputs.
The experimental results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ exhibits superior performance compared to S-ICOCO and other baselines in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability

\title{Scientific Review Agents: A Step Towards Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Peers}

\begin{abstract}
In this study, we are exploring the design of an AI agent capable of providing high-quality feedback on scientific papers, the ability to effectively engage in multi-turn communications, and autonomously evaluating papers based on obtained feedback.
To accomplish these objectives, we introduce S-ICOCO+, an enhanced agent that extends the capabilities of S-ICOCO.\footnote{The outline of S-ICOCO follows the format described by \citet{tyser2024ai}: ``First, the model recommends to accept or reject this paper. Then, the model provides comments for the authors to raise their science-related issues or concerns. Finally, the model evaluates the paper based on its own outlooks based on the comments.''}
Our approach involves integrating key attributes of peer reviews in the training data and improving the algorithms to optimize feedback quality.
We carry out an extensive collection of subjective metrics regarding generated comments and comments-based evaluations, as well as objective metrics regarding acceptance/rejection recommendations, which allows for a thorough assessment of the generated outputs.
The experimental results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ exhibits superior performance compared to S-ICOCO and other baselines in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}



\begin{comment}
One of the key steps towards autonomous AI agents is building an AI-peer which can provide valuable comments on scientific papers and make recommendations on their further improvements. In recent years, we have seen various works exploring different aspects of AI-assisted scientific peer review~\cite{Hu2024AutomatedDO}.
For example, some works focus on enhancing the recommendation of acceptance/rejection~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,su2024analysisicml2023ranking}, or treating the feedback for the authors~\cite{tyser2024ai,robertson2023gpt4,kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent}, or replacing human's effort in the peer review~\cite{liu2023reviewergpt}. Recently, a comprehensive survey and evaluation of AI-peers were conducted~\cite{tyser2024ai}, where S-ICOCO, a Balanced Reward Optimization~\cite{pang2024iterative} algorithm using Chain-of-Thought (CoT)\cite{wei2022chain} as prompt, was pointed out as the best approach over others for AI-assisted paper review.

This paper builds on such work and investigates the further possibilities to advance the AI-peer. S-ICOCO+ not only integrates the broader aspects of scientific peer review but also enhances the algorithms to optimize feedback quality in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
To achieve these, we improve S-ICOCO at three levels.
Firstly, in contrast to S-ICOCO, which only learns from Heuristic Reward Optimization (HRO~\cite{Hinton06}), we integrate the key attributes of peer reviews defined by ~\citealt{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}, including correctness, clarity, expertise, relevance, clarity, completeness, conciseness, and relevance to the author's work, into the training data. The peer reviews\footnote{We utilize the papers reviewed by authors from prestigious institutions such as MIT and Harvard.} are collected from ~\citealt{jin2024agentreivewexploringpeerreview}, along withheuristic feedback from ICML papers and comments on ICML papers by ICML authors on social media. We analyze the common expressions of high-quality feedback and summarize them as rules. The summary rules are used to construct the heuristic reward function for the generator.
Secondly, we improve the reward optimization algorithm from S-ICOCO to optimize the feedback quality of the generator. In addition to the Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) method used in S-ICOCO, we adopt Balanced Reward Optimization (IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}). In addition, we further introduce Iterative Reward Optimization (IPO) as the main reward optimization algorithm for its ability to adapt to various reward models and its superior performance.

\end{comment} 
In recent years, the field of AI-assisted scientific paper review has seen significant advancements~\cite{Hu2024AutomatedDO,wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient}, including methods that enhance individual aspects such as paper feedback~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,tyser2024ai,robertson2023gpt4}, recommendation and rejection~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,su2024analysisicml2023ranking,kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent}, and replacing human's effort in the peer review~\cite{liu2023reviewergpt}.
Among these, \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a comprehensive benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO\footnote{S-ICOCO (``Scientific Information CONtent based Commentor, with Chain of Thought'') was the best approach in their experiments.} as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
This paper builds on such work and investigates the possibilities to further advance the AI peer.
S-ICOCO+ not only integrates broader aspects of peer review \cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} into the training data but also enhances the algorithms to optimize feedback quality in various aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
To achieve these, we improve S-ICOCO at three levels.
Firstly, in contrast to S-ICOCO, which only learns from Heuristic Reward Optimization (HRO~\cite{Hinton06}), we integrate the key attributes of peer reviews defined by \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}—correctness, clarity, expertise, relevance, completeness, conciseness, and relevance to the author's work—in the training data.
The peer reviews are collected from prestigious institutions such as MIT and Harvard, which author(s) of papers have reviewed and left comments on social media.
Additionally, the comments on ICML papers by their authors from social media are also gathered.
The common expressions of high-quality feedback are extracted as rules after analyzing the training data.
These rules are used to construct the heuristic reward function for the generator.
Secondly, we improve the reward optimization algorithm from S-ICOCO to optimize the feedback quality of the generator.
In addition to the Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) method used in S-ICOCO, we adopt Balanced Reward Optimization (IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}) to enhance the reasoning ability and expression of the generator.
In addition to this, we find that reinforcement learning with Iterative Reward Optimization (IPO) as the reward model can further enhance the generator's reasoning ability, the expression of generated feedback, and the overall quality of the feedback.
Lastly, we design a number of self-verification methods to ensure S-ICOCO+ stay up to date and adhere to the ethical norms of the peer review community.
The generated outputs are extensively subjectively and objectively evaluated by 37 researchers, including 31 NLP and AI researchers and 6 reviewers of ACL papers. In particular, S-ICOCO+, S-ICOCO, and other baselines are asked to generate comments-based evaluations with several seed comments generated by humans. The results demonstrate that S-ICOCO+ exhibits superior performance compared to other baselines regarding expression and generalizability. When compared to S-ICOCO, S-ICOCO+ shows significant improvements in all aspects, including reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
In summary, our contributions in this paper include:
\begin{itemize}
\item We carry out an extensive collection of subjective metrics regarding generated comments and comments-based evaluations, as well as objective metrics regarding acceptance/rejection recommendations, which allows for a thorough assessment of the generated outputs.
\item We develop S-ICOCO+, an AI agent that automates the automatic peer review of scientific papers, which outperforms other baselines regarding expression and generalizability, and outperforms S-ICOCO regarding reasoning ability, expression, and generalizability.
\item We form high-quality peer-review training data by extracting the attributes defined by ~\citealt{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} from reviews by peer reviewers and construct the heuristic reward function based on various analysis and experiments. The training data and the heuristic reward function can facilitate the development of future AI-assisted scientific paper review agents.
\end{itemize}



\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Computational Scientific Discovery}
The goal of computational scientific research is to accelerate discovery with the use of computational tools and artificial intelligence, which has shown promise in speeding up scientific discovery in areas such as materials science, biology, and chemistry~\cite{langley2024integrated}.
\citet{jumper2021highly} applied deep learning to accelerate discovery and beat nature in simulating the structures of proteins, which has earned a Nobel Prize for biology.
\citet{romera2024mathematical} used large language models to discover new mathematical proofs.
\citet{hayes2024simulating} used deep reinforcement learning to simulate evolution.
Since the early days of computational science, researchers have explored AI-assisted solutions to accelerate discovery, including data-driven models in chemistry and material science~\cite{pyzer2022accelerating,merchant2023scaling}, and AI-driven simulation and hypothesis generation in biology and genetics~\cite{hayes2024simulating,jumper2021highly,buchanan1981dendral}. 
Ever since the late 1960s, computational scientific research has been exploring automated analytical tools to accelerate discovery~\cite{langley1987scientific,langley2024integrated}.
However, the exploration of computational paper review to speed up the scientific paper publication process is still in its early stages.
\subsection{Computational Paper Review}
In the early days, researchers built systems to create new mathematical and computer science knowledge, such as new algorithms, new program routines, and new theories.
\citet{lenat1977automated} used computational methods to create new results in mathematics such as tree algorithms.
\citet{hutter2001towards} learned, generalized and composed new knowledge to do heuristic reasoning.
\citet{lenat1983eurisko} created new knowledge including heuristics, domain concepts, and terminology.
\citet{buchanan1981dendral} built a system to streamline the analysis of organic compounds and attempt to find ways to predict a molecule's properties from its structure.
However, despite considerable interest in automatically reviewing scientific papers, only a few works have been done to research in this topic~\cite{wang2023scientific}. Recently, \citet{liang2024mapping} conducted a study to map out the usage of large language models (LLMs) in scientific papers. In addition, \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
\subsection{LLM-based Paper Review Generation}
The rapid advancements in LLM technology have prompted various studies to explore the application of LLM technologies to the peer review process.
These methods can be broadly categorized into two types: those that enhance the reviewer's ability to draft scientific papers~\cite{oberg2022teaching,smith2006peer,boughton2018research}, and those that employ AI technologies to assist in the peer review process~\cite{li2024ai4r,tyser2024ai,du2024llms,kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent}.
Specifically, AI-assisted scientific paper review has recently captured considerable attention.
\citet{liu2023reviewergpt} proposed an exploratory study to use LLM to generate reviews, but only achieved limited success.
\citet{robertson2023gpt4} demonstrated the potential of GPT-4\cite{achiam2023gpt} to generate high-quality reviews, but the study was limited to a single case study without explicitly designing models to generate review. \citet{zhang2022investigating} employed LLMs to increase the fairness and diversity of the peer review process.
\citet{hu2022lora} introduced LoRA\cite{hu2022lora} to fine-tune LLMs to assist with the paper peer review process.
\citet{kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent} applied a low-rank, all-to-non-all approximation~\cite{wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient} of deep learning models in the peer review process to achieve higher performance.
\citet{du2024llms} proposed a two-stage approach to revise the draft of the paper by leveraging LLMs.
\citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a comprehensive benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO, an agent using CoT~\cite{wei2022chain} prompting to achieve better reasoning results, as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review.
\subsection{Reward Model}
Reward models have been extensively employed to evaluate the value of actions in various sequential decision-making problems such as video games and reinforcement learning. See \citet{pang2024iterative} for a more comprehensive review of related works.
\citet{NEURIPS2023_91f18a12} introduced GPT-4 level reward models for reinforcement learning based on LLMs.
\citet{lambert2024rewardbench} proposed a set of tasks for benchmarking reward models. \citet{yang2024collaborative} introduced a new iterative reward optimization algorithm to achieve superior performance compared to other reward optimization algorithms.
\citet{rafailov2023direct} proposed an algorithm that aligned the output of a language model with the preference of human and introduced DPO as an alternative approach to RLHF. SimPO~\cite{meng2024simposimplepreferenceoptimization}, IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}, and IPO-Rec~\cite{yang2024collaborative} are the state-of-the-art iterative reward model optimization algorithms, which show superior performance compared to the previous approaches such as DPO. In this paper, IPO is introduced as the reward optimization algorithm to train the generator after SFT since it has a greater ability to adapt to various reward models and it shows superior performance in the experiments.

S-ICOCO+ is a well-trained AI agent that can automatically provide comments on scientific papers and make recommendations for acceptance or rejection. The method of S-ICOCO+ is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:method}. In contrast to S-ICOCO, which only learns from heuristic data and accepted papers, S-ICOCO+ incorporates a variety of peer reviews into the training process, including balanced review data (highly rated and lowly rated), incomplete review data, concise review data, and detailed review data. Additionally, rules are extracted and integrated into the training process to guide the generator towards producing high-quality feedback. S-ICOCO+ can not only generate comments on the authors' addressed papers but also further provide comments on the addressed papers to further improve the quality of the authors' work based on the initial comments.

\subsection{Data Construction}
We utilize \texttt{gpt-4-0613}~\cite{achiam2023gpt} to extract key review expressions from review texts and to reformat the output format. In the subsequent steps 2 to 5, we construct various types of peer reviews, including balanced review data, incomplete review data, concise review data, and detailed review data. In step 6, we construct the seed comments with the extracted expressions and training data. More details on each step can be found in the subsequent text.
\paragraph{Step 1: Extract key review expressions from peer reviews.}
We use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to extract key review phrases from peer review texts. In particular, we design a prompt that is a combination of a system prompt and a user prompt. The system prompt includes details such as the reviewer's position, the reviewer's expertise, the rating (i.e., 1 for accept, 2 for minor, 3 for major) that the reviewer gives for the paper, and the name of the paper's conference. The user prompt includes a task description and a format definition. To provide more context to the model, we provide a number of sample review texts as history in the user prompt. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to extract key expressions from the peer review texts. In addition to this, we define a number of key aspects including Relevancy, Feasibility, Technique Quality, Accuracy, Grounding, Gaps and limitations, and Improvements and suggested changes. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate a list of expressions for each key aspect. A total of 116 expressions are generated regarding the 7 key aspects.
\paragraph{Step 2: Construct balanced review data.}
We use the peer reviews of ICML papers since we find that these are the most easy to obtain and relevant, as they are publicly available. In particular, we use the papers and reviews from ICML 2023. Specifically, the papers and their annotated reviews are crawled from the \href{https://www.icml2023conference.com/papers_and_papers.html}{official website} of ICML 2023. We use this data to construct the balanced review data. In particular, we find that the review comments on ICML papers have three properties. The first is that they are mostly positive. The second is that they are very detailed and not very concise. The third is that they often have typos and missing numbers, which are common in expert comments~\cite{nuijten2016prevalence}. The properties of the reviews may affect the quality of the output of the generator. Therefore, we use the extracted key expressions from Step 1 to construct the balanced review data. Since the ratings are common in our analysis of the reviews, we use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate balancer ratings (i.e., half of 1, 2, and 3 with equal proportion) for each review. In addition, we ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to correct the typos in the reviews. The prompt of \texttt{gpt-4-0613} includes a task description, a2e conversion rule, a guidance of rating, and the review to be modified. With the help of the key expressions, the ratings and the typos in the reviews, the \texttt{gpt-4-0613} can generate high-quality reviews with balanced ratings and less typos.
\paragraph{Step 3: Construct incomplete review data.}
In the data construction of the incomplete review data, we first define five types of incomplete reviews: missing Strengths, missing Limitations, missing Letters, missing Outlines, and missing Ratings. Missing Letters represents review data that only lack certain letters. In the peer review, the reviewers should assign letter-based feedback (e.g., L1, L2, and so on) to each point corresponding to the focus of the paper. In real review data, the ratings may not match the ratio 1:2:1. To address this, we category the review ratings and missing ratings as one type of incomplete review data. Ultimately, we generate a total of 78,787 incomplete review data points through the data construction process.
\paragraph{Step 4: Construct concise review data.}
We find that peer reviews are often incomplete and not very concise. Concise data refers to review data that only have missing outlines. In this step, we use \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate a concise version of the review with the rating assigned by \texttt{gpt-4-0613}. Similar to the last step, the prompt includes a task description, a guidance of rating, and the original review. We find that \texttt{gpt-4-0613} can generate high-quality, appropriately lengthy (not too long and not too short), and appropriate format reviews with the extracted key expressions from Step 1.
\paragraph{Step 5: Construct detailed review data.}
In this step, we add details to the concise data from Step 4 to form detailed reviews. In particular, the detailed review data not only has a detailed positive aspect but also a detailed negative aspect. We ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate detailed content for Strengths and Limitations using the extracted key expressions from Step 1. In this step, we generate positive detailed review data. Then, we ask \texttt{gpt-4-0613} to generate detailed positive and negative expressions for Strengths and Limitations respectively. Finally, we generate the negative detailed review data using the detailed negative expressions. Using these expressions, we can randomly select expressions to form detailed incomplete review data.
\paragraph{Step 6: Construct seed comments.}
We randomly select the seed comments from the generated data. In particular, we use seed comments generated by humans and S-ICOCO+. The prompt for generating seed comments includes a description of the generation method, the rating, the paper's content, and so on. Specifically, for S-ICOCO+, the prompt also includes the responses of S-ICOCO+ to the comments generated by humans in Step 1 to Step 5. Additionally, the papers are randomly selected from papers at the \href{https://arxiv.org/list/mathcis?sort&show=300}{arXiv Maths, Logic and Computational Systems category, and the sub-categories of the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning sub-category.


\subsection{Pre-training}
The model used in S-ICOCO+ is \texttt{Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1}. In addition to Mistral~\cite{jiang2023mistral}, we also explore \texttt{GPT4-Preview-Turbo} and Qwen~\cite{yqwen2.5} as the base generators.

\subsection{Supervised Fine-tuning}

In this phase, the generator is fine-tuned using the heuristic data and the balanced review data collected in Step 2. In particular, in addition to Mistral-7b, OPT-12G and LLaMA3-8B are also explored as the base model for supervised fine-tuning. The supervised fine-tuning aims to ensure that the generator learns to format high-quality feedback and assign appropriate ratings to papers. To this end, we use the ratings as the objective signal for supervised fine-tuning. In this step, we also use the heuristic feedback in S-ICOCO and the feedback generated by \texttt{gpt-4-0613} based on the reviews extracted in Step 1 and Step 2. The prompt for supervised fine-tuning includes details of the task and the output format.

\subsection{Reward Model Fine-tuning}
Since we find that in Step 7, both LLaMA3-8B and GPT4-Preview-Turbo perform worse than Mistral-7b, we choose Mistral-7b as the base model for supervised fine-tuning and further reward optimization fine-tuning. In this step, we fine-tune the generator with the reward optimization algorithm. In particular, S-ICOCO uses an balanced reward optimization algorithm based on CoT to optimize the generator. In this step, we find that using this approach, the generator's reasoning ability is significantly improved. S-ICOCO+ uses the Iterative Reward Optimization (IPO)~\cite{pang2024iterative} algorithm to optimize the generator, which demonstrate superior performance compared to other reward model optimization algorithms. In this paper, we show that using IPO, the generator's reasoning ability is further improved, and the expression of the output is significantly enhanced. The prompt for reward optimization fine-tuning includes details of the task and the output format. The training process continues until convergence or until it reaches a maximum number of training steps.
\subsection{Self-verification}
In the self-verification methods, we introduce various constraints to restrict the output of the generator in order to meet the requirements of the peer review process. In particular, we use a detector \cite{bao2021predicting,zhu2024locking} to detect whether the generator's responses contain any keywords defined by reviewers. If the detector detects any such words, the generator will reconstruct its response. In addition, we also use the Prompt-seeding method \cite{hu2024automated} to prevent the generator from deviating from the seed prompt, thus ensuring that the generator maintains high consistency with the seed prompt. With the self-verification methods, the outputs of the generator can be of higher quality and meet the requirements of the peer review process.

\subsection{Inference}
In the inference phase, the generator is prompted to input the paper's content, the task, and the previous corresponding history to the model. The generator will generate the corresponding response to the prompt. In this process, the generator will go through the inference stage three times. In the first stage, the generator recommends whether to accept or reject the paper. In the second stage, the generator generates the main comment. In the third stage, based on the history of the comments generated in the first stage, the generator will further provide more detailed comments to evaluate the paper.



\section{Experiment}


\subsection{Objective Metric}
To evaluate the ability of S-ICOCO+ to provide comments-based evaluations, we conduct an extensive experiment to subjectively evaluate the generated comments-based evaluations with several seed comments generated by humans.
In this experiment, S-ICOCO+, S-ICOCO, CoT~\cite{wei2022chain}, and chain-of-reflection~\cite{zhang2024generative} are used to generate comments-based evaluation. 37 participants (including 31 NLP and AI researchers, and 6 reviewers of ACL papers) from prestigious institutions such as MIT and Harvard are employed to evaluate the comments-based evaluations. In the evaluation, each participant is tasked to rate the comments-based-evaluations scored from 1 to 10.\footnote{More details about the experiment can be found in \cref{app:objective-metric}.}
In addition to the above, we use several objective metrics to evaluate the ability of S-ICOCO+ to recommend acceptance and rejection of papers and the ability of S-ICOCO+ to provide feedback for authors's paper. The metrics are defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Acceptance.} It is measured as the formula $\mathrm{Accuracy= (1\times\mathrm{Recall}) / (1\times\mathrm{Recall}+1\times\mathrm{Precision})}$, where $\mathrm{Recall}$ represents the ability of the generator to provide comments on important content, and $\mathrm{Precision}$ represents the ability of the generator to avoid generating irrelevant comments.

\item \textbf{Coverage.} It is measured as the percentage of the accepted papers covered by the generator's comments. The formula is $\mathrm{Coverage= (1\times\mathrm{Accept}) / (\mathrm{Accept+papers\ not\ covered})}$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Subjective Metric}
The 37 participants are asked to rate \citealt{collins2017supervised} papers and the papers selected in \citealt{tyser2024ai}. More details about the papers can be found in \cref{sec:selected-papers}. Each participant is asked to rate the comments-based-evaluations based on the \textit{consensus} of the peer review community and the \textit{rules} defined by ACL.\footnote{\href{https://acl-online.org//www.acl-climbing.net/AutoP/acl2024-colour.html}{acl.org/2024-climbing/acl}} The rules represent and summarize the criteria that the peer review community commonly agrees on.
\paragraph{Overall Results}
