\section{Related Works}

\subsection{Automatic Paper Review}
In recent years, various works have explored different aspects of AI-assisted scientific paper review.
For example, \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} proposed a model that improves the ranking and acceptance decision accuracy in NLP paper review. Their method is a reinforcement learning framework under the contrastive learning. \citet{NEURIPS2020_6b493230} also demonstrated that a small model can be trained to provide useful feedback for paper revision. \citet{su2024analysisicml2023ranking} explored using reinforcement learning to reward-model the paper ranking process. They showed that using a two-policy Clarkes similarity strategy based on contrasting features of papers can generate high-quality rankings. \citet{tyser2024ai} conducted a benchmark on various AI agents and pointed out S-ICOCO, an agent using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT)~\cite{wei2022chain} prompting to achieve better reasoning results, as the best approach for AI-assisted paper review. 
\citet{liu2023reviewergpt} proposed a exploratory study to use LLM to generate reviews, but only achieved limited success. \citet{zhang2022investigating} employed LLMs to increase the fairness and diversity of the peer review process. They used an ensemble of random forest or SVMs to evaluate the correlation between various features and the review outcome, and they used the decision trees to assign labels for papers. \citet{hu2022lora} introduced LoRA to fine-tune LLMs to assist with the paper review process. They showed that the generator can provide valuable feedback for paper revision. \citet{kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowerexponent} applied a low-rank, all-to-none approximation of deep learning models in the peer review process to achieve higher performance. They showed that the generator can help with paper feedback. In addition, \citet{li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning} showed that LLM as a Co-Pilot can effectively assist in the generation of machine learning experiments. \citet{baek2024researchagent} introduced an idea agent that can freely iterate idea between paper topics, and literature, and then refine these ideas.
\subsection{Reward Model}
Reward models have been extensively employed to evaluate the value of actions in various sequential decision-making problems such as video games and reinforcement learning. See \citealt{pang2024iterative} for a more comprehensive review of related works. \citet{achiam2023gpt} demonstrated the potential of GPT-4 for reward modeling through next-token prediction. They showed that the generated rewards closely aligned with human preferences, and the reward scores were on par with those of GPT-4-Turbo. \citet{NEURIPS2023_91f18a12} introduced GPT-4 level reward models for reinforcement learning based on LLMs. \citet{lambert2024rewardbench} proposed a set of tasks for benchmarking reward models. They showed that the reward models were often limited to high-level, human-like understanding and reasoning. The reward models were not always consistent or reliable across various scenarios. The development of reward models remained a significant challenge. In particular, they found that GPT-4 and Mistral-7B were well-suited as reward models. \citet{rafailov2023direct} proposed an algorithm that aligned the output of a language model with the preference of human and introduced DPO as an alternative approach to RLHF. SimPO~\cite{meng2024simposimplepreferenceoptimization}, IPO~\cite{pang2024iterative}, and IPO-Rec~\cite{yang2024collaborative} are the state-of-the-art iterative reward optimization algorithm, which show superior performance compared to other reward optimization algorithms. In particular, IPO shows superior performance and is more adaptable to various reward models than other reward optimization algorithms. In addition, IPO-Rec proposes methods to optimize the reward model to enhance the consistency between the generator's output and the original dataset. \citet{xiong2024iterativepreferencelearninghuman} provided a comprehensive benchmark on preference learning based on human feedback (RLHF), and iterative preference learning human feedback (IPO). They showed that IPO has better adaptability than RLHF because IPO is adaptable to various reward models. In particular, \citet{an2023learning} found that IPO can enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs. In their experiment, they used GPT-4 as the seed generator and then used IPO to train a new GPT-4. They found that the new GPT-4 had better reasoning abilities than GPT-4. In their later work, \citet{yuan2024self} used IPO to iteratively train the new GPT-4. They found that the new GPT-4 had better reasoning abilities than the old GPT-4. In their later work, they showed that the new GPT-4 has better reasoning abilities than the old GPT-4. In their later work, they used IPO to train a Mistral-7B~\cite{jiang2023mistral}, and found that IPO significantly enhanced the reasoning ability of Mistral-7B.


\section{Conclusion}

In this paper, we develop S-ICOCO+, an AI agent that automatically provides comments on scientific paper, and recommends acceptance or rejection of scientific papers. In the experiments, S-ICOCO+ demonstrates superior ability regarding reasoning, expression, and generalizability.



\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{Artificial Separation of Strengths and Limitations}
During the training and evaluation processes, we manually separate the strengths and limitations of the paper. However, in real-life scenarios, reviewers often do not explicitly distinguish between strengths and limitations. S-ICOCO+ tends to identify weak points as limitations and strong points as strengths. In the paper feedback generation phase, S-ICOCO+ tends to refer to weak points as limitations and strong points as strengths. This could be due to the prompts used for both heuristic data generation and reference comment generation, which separate strengths and weaknesses of papers. We will conduct further research to reduce the reliance on manual separation of papers in future work.
\paragraph{Artificial Separation of Recommended and Not Recommended Papers}
During the training and evaluation processes, we manually divide the accepted papers and rejected papers into two categories. However, during the evaluation process, it is impossible to divide the papers into two categories. S-ICOCO+ tends to divide the papers into two categories: recommended and not recommended. In the paper feedback generation phase, S-ICOCO+ tends to provide reasons for not recommending the paper as feedback to the author. This could be due to the design of the prompts for both training data generation and reference comment generation, which separate the papers into recommended and not recommended categories. We will conduct further research to reduce the reliance on manual separation of paper categories in future work.

\section{Introduction}


Researchers have long dreamt of artificial intelligence (AI) agents capable of scientific discovery \cite{langley1987scientific}. Existing AI agents for scientific discovery typically follow a paradigm that includes three stages: idea proposal, design and review \cite{langley2024integrated, wang2024scientific}. In these three stages, AI agents generate candidate scientific ideas and then evaluate these ideas based on experimental evidence to determine their importance and potential impact \cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,liang2024mapping,liu2024towards,hayes2024simulating}. 
Researchers at Google recently used AI agents to create a new machine learning method, referred to as "raw neural network" or "rnn", which has a comparable level of sophistication as a human-designed method \cite{reid2024gemini}. Other researchers have also explored the possibility of autonomous discovery by focusing on idea proposal or proposal improvement in fields such as chemistry \cite{Hu2024AutomatedDO}, mathematics \cite{romera2024mathematical}, surveys \cite{wang2024autosurvey}, materials science \cite{pyzer2022accelerating}, chemistry \cite{merchant2023scaling} and biology \cite{hayes2024simulating}.




Early research on AI agents for scientific discovery has primarily focused on the ideas generation stage. For example, AIScient \cite{lu2024ai} proposes the concept of automated scientific discovery and develops an autonomous system. Similarly, MLR-Copilot \cite{li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning} presents a comprehensive system for autonomous machine learning research that operates through a closed-loop process. Scientific Idea Generation \cite{radensky2024scideator} introduces a novel method for generating scientific ideas and demonstrates the effectiveness of large language models in automatically proposing and disseminating ideas. Similarly, ReAgent \cite{baek2024researchagent} proposes a research agent design that iteratively refines and outputs more accurate research topic ideas by considering topics retrieved from previous iterations. Furthermore, MLAgentBench \cite{huang2024mlagentbench} studies how language agents can assist various machine learning research processes and proposes a benchmark for evaluating the performance of such agent systems. While these works mainly focus on synthesizing proposals, another research direction explores algorithmic design for proposal improvement \cite{fang2024autonomous,salim2024proposalgpt,zhang2024generative}.

The evaluation stage, which determines the usefulness of candidate scientific ideas, is also crucial for completing the loop of scientific discovery. However, this portion of the research pipeline has received less attention. ReviewGPT and its subsequent versions \cite{liu2023reviewergpt,tyser2024ai,du2024llms}, which have studied peer review for ideas, begin the exploration.
Furthermore,  AI4Review \cite{jin2024agentreivewexploringpeerreview}  investigates multi-agent systems for reviewing scientific papers. This system has been shown to effectively improve review quality, increase review efficiency, and enhance the consistency of feedback. Additionally, SCAIMon \cite{wang2023scimon} introduces a reward signal for proposing ideas that are more novel, non-trivial and their impacts can be. This reward signal plays an important role in selecting the best ideas through iterations. RewardBench \cite{lambert2024rewardbench} proposes a large-scale reward benchmark for evaluating the ability of reward models to rank suggestions, and investigates various aspects of ranking quality. 
Despite significant progress, these AI agents for scientific discovery often follow a static, sequential pipeline, where each stage adheres to fixed rules. Such approaches may inherently be inconsistent with human research processes, which typically involve iterative updates and improvements \cite{oberg2022teaching}. By recording prior ideas and methods, humans can concurrently make concurrent discoveries and exploit synergy among different stages. 



In this paper, we introduce an iterative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for autonomous scientific discovery, shown in Fig \ref{fig:overview}. This framework is closely inspired by human scientific collaboration, aiming to expand the scale of output while simultaneously enhancing the quality of discovered science. \section{Preliminaries}


\textbf{Fine-Tuning a language model:}
Language models, such as BERT \cite{Hinton06}, GPT \cite{achiam2023gpt}, and Mistral \cite{jiang2023mistral}, which are fine-tuned by maximizing the log likelihood of prediction \cite{goodfellow2016deep}, have demonstrated the potential to interact with users and assist them in completing tasks. These models are typically trained in a supervised manner, using dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y)\}$, where $y$ is the corresponding completion of $x$. This type of tuning is referred to as ``supervised fine-tuning" \cite{hu2022lora, kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowertrain, wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient}. 
The aim of supervised fine-tuning is to foresee and anticipate the user's needs, ensuring that the model's outputs are consistent and useful to users. However, supervised fine-tuning may not be the most effective approach when it comes to optimizing a system consisting of multiple agents. Each agent seeks to maximize their own utility, and therefore, may seek to maximize the gap between their actions and actions that are expected by other agents. In other words, they may even take actions that are detrimental to other agents. For example, in the context of review agents, the preference feedback they obtain may appear to lack credibility if the language model is used as the supervised fine-tuning method.
\textbf{RLHF:} reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) leverages reinforcement learning to train language models to better align with human input, thereby improving user experience \cite{ouyang2022training, openai2023gpt4}. An auxiliary reward model is trained in RLHF using human preference feedback to assess the quality of generated sentences. Traditional RLHF typically involves three models: a policy model, a reward model, and a reference model. The reward model is trained based on human feedback on positive and negative sentence completions. The policy model is then fine-tuned using reinforcement learning to maximize the reward provided by the reward model.

\textbf{RL:} reinforcement learning (RL) trains a policy model, $\pi$, to maximize expected reward \cite{sutton2018reinforcement, Hinton06, lecun2015deep}. In the context of RL, a policy model, $\pi$, generates an action, $a_t$, at time step $t$, based on its interpretation of the state, $s_t$, of the environment. Each action has an associated reward, $r(s_t, a_t)$, that is predetermined and may vary over time. The objective of the policy model is to maximize the sum of rewards, calculated as the expected reward over time, formulated as:
$
\label{lossgpt} \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t \geq 0}[R(\pi;\pi_t)]
$,
where $R(\pi;\pi_t)=\sum_{t}{r(s_t,a_t)}$ denotes the expected sum of rewards up to time step $t$
\textbf{In the context of preference learning:} $
    \mathcal{L} = -\alpha \mathbb{E}_{(x,y^1,y^2)}\log P_\theta(y^1\mid x) - \mathbb{E}_{(x,y^1,y^2)}\log P_\theta(y^2\mid x) \label{lossgpt}$,
where $P_\theta$ is a language model parameterized by $\theta$, $\alpha$ denotes a tuning parameter used to adjust the cross-entropy loss for the preferred completion, $y^1$, either $y^1$ or $y^2$, given the context $x$. The loss is adjusted to fit the sampled data by adjusting $\alpha$ \cite{rafailov2023direct, zhu2024safetylock}.





\section{Method}

Modeling the scientific research process as a series of actions and reactions, we can view the process of proposing, designing, and reviewing proposals as a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problem \cite{lowe2017multi, Hu2024AutomatedDO}. In this framework, agents engage asynchronously to drive the next stage of the research process based on the results of previous agents. Each agent can be regarded as a policy model, denoted by $\pi_\chi$, which is capable of generating outputs that can be interpreted as possible choices for actions in the research process according to the current state of the environment. These agents are capable of generating and evaluating scientific knowledge proposals. Our goal is to enhance the capacity of the entire system to make better proposals. This requires improving the policy models based on the evaluation results obtained from the most recent round of proposals, as represented by the current state. If one policy model is improved, the overall system is enhanced. To achieve this, we make all policy models learn from their own experiences. We call the proposed method Iterative Multi-agent Preference Optimization (IMPO), and the framework is shown in Figure \ref{fig:main_and_code} (a).
\subsection{Multi-agent System}
\label{multi-agent system}
\textbf{Agent systems consist of three types of agents.} Depending on their roles, agents can be categorized into three types: any ideas that are spontaneously emerged in brain (raw insights, "raw neural network," etc.) or formed by conventional methods (experiments, analyses, hypotheses, etc.) as proposal agents (AS), any methods that are spontaneously emerged in brain (raw insights, "raw neural network," etc.) or formed by conventional methods (theoretical designs, designs based on practice, hypothesis testing, etc.) as design agents (RA), and any criteria that can improve, verify, or validate newly proposed ideas as review agents (AR). Besides, we introduce two types of "environment": journals that act as AS and peers that act as AR.
\textbf{Protocols for agent communication.} All policy models alternatively propose suggestions, critique these suggestions, or use them as a basis for further suggestions. If a policy model is selected as the final "output" (i.e., it chosen as the "winning" suggestion) in a round of exploration, it receives a positive reward signal, denoted by $y^1$. Conversely, other policy models that did not outperform the "winning" suggestion receive a negative reward signal, denoted by $y^2$. The evaluation of which proposal wins the current round is based on our domain for chemistry in this paper, and detailed rules are provided in Section \ref{evaluation} Marketing any feedback from AR and AS as a preference dataset to AR. Throughout the entire research loop, policy model $\pi_\chi$ will have multiple opportunities to learn the feedback related to suggestions they have made and subsequently enhance their understanding of those suggestions.

\subsection{Iterative Update} 
\label{framework}
\textbf{Fine-tune on the preference dataset:} We deploy the feedback from reviewers that is converted by Section \ref{multi-agent system} to train a reward model \cite{an2023learning}, which is then used to fine-tune the policy model \cite{yuan2024self}. At the beginning of the $n$-th iteration, the preference dataset used for training the policy model is initialized as \(\mathcal{D}_0^1, \mathcal{D}_0^2, ..., \mathcal{D}_0^K\), where \(\mathcal{D}_0^1\) to \(\mathcal{D}_0^K\) represent the datasets for the three types of agents, specifically for $\pi_\mathrm{AS}$, \(\pi_\mathrm{RA}\), and \(\pi_\mathrm{AR}\), respectively.

At the $n$-th iteration, after the exploration of the environment, an updated preference dataset is obtained. The feedback from AR and AS on proposals of $\pi_\mathrm{RA}$ and $\pi_\mathrm{AS}$ is converted to preference dataset and added into $\mathcal{D}_n^1, \mathcal{D}_n^2, ..., \mathcal{D}_n^K$, respectively.
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal{D}_{n+1}^1 := \mathcal{D}_n^1 \cup \mathcal{D}_{feedback}^{SA}; \quad \mathcal{D}_{n+1}^2 := \mathcal{D}_n^2 \cup \mathcal{D}_{feedback}^{RA};  \quad \mathcal{D}_{n+1}^3 := \mathcal{D}_{n}^3 \cup \mathcal{D}_{feedback}^{AR}.
\end{equation*}

Upon completion of the $n$-th iteration of the system, the policy model generates suggestions based on its current knowledge, represented as $(\hat{y}_{proposal}^n, \hat{y}_{ref}^n)=\pi_\chi(\cdot\mid s_n)$, where $\pi_\chi$ can be $\pi_\mathrm{AS}$, $\pi_\mathrm{RA}$ or $\pi_\mathrm{AR}$. The suggestion, $\hat{y}_{proposal}^n$, evolves over time as the policy model learns from the environment.

This process is repeated for $N$ iterations, and the updates to the three types of agents from iteration $n$ to iteration $n+1$ are as follows:
\begin{equation*}
    \pi_{\mathrm{AS}}^{n+1} := \underset{\pi_{\mathrm{AS}}'}{\arg\max} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^1}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{AS},\phi}(y^1 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{AS}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{AS}}] - \alpha_1 \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^1}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{AS},\phi}(y^2 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{AS}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{AS}}],
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
    \pi_{\mathrm{RA}}^{n+1} := \underset{\pi_{\mathrm{RA}}'}{\arg\max} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^2}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{RA},\phi}(y^1 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{RA}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{RA}}] - \alpha_2 \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^2}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{RA},\phi}(y^2 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{RA}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{RA}}],
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
    \pi_{\mathrm{AR}}^{n+1} := \underset{\pi_{\mathrm{AR}}'}{\arg\max} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^3}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{AR},\phi}(y^1 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{AR}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{AR}}] - \alpha_3 \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n+1}^3}[P_{\pi_\mathrm{AR},\phi}(y^2 | a ; \pi_\mathrm{AR}'(\cdot | s_n)) a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{AR}}].
\end{equation*}

where $\phi$ is the reward signal.

\subsection{Evaluation}
\label{evaluation}
We are now prepared to elaborate on the conduct of the experiments and the assessment of the proposed method. 
Given that there are multiple ways of improving our three agents, a comprehensive evaluation is necessary. 
This involves evaluating the quality of the proposals and the soundness of the review criteria, while also considering the relationships among agents such as collaboration and interactions. 
Here we explain how we do the evaluation of the proposed method and give more details of each agent.
\textbf{Evaluation metrics.} To access the effectiveness and trustworthiness of our proposed framework, we focus on following three key points:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, noitemsep]
\item Quality of proposed ideas by $\pi_\mathrm{AS}$ and $\pi_\mathrm{RA}$ (the more, the better);
\item Relevance and usefulness of reviewed criteria by $\pi_\mathrm{AR}$ (the higher, the better);
\item $\pi_{\mathrm{AS}}$ and $\pi_\mathrm{RA}$ are learned and evolved from the fine-tuned method \cite{rafailov2023direct} and not the naive prompt-based method.
\end{itemize}

Next, we describe the design of three evaluation aspects of result in Section \ref{feedback}.

\textbf{Quality of proposed ideas.} 
In this paper, we use a combination of metrics to assess the quality of proposed ideas. These metrics include three high-level criteria for idea quality: Novelty, Benefial, and Availability. Annotating each proposal in a four-way scheme, similar to \citet{su2024analysisicml2023ranking}, we select the most fitting option for each criterion from the following choices: "Yes (strong), No (strong), No (weak), Yes (weak), and Uncertain." 
The options are selected based on a scale of preference, indicating the strength of their alignment with each criterion.
Then, we can get four matrices, \(M_0\) to \(M_3\). We transform \(M_0\) to \(M_0'\) by decomposing \(M_0\) into distinct vectors \(\vec{v}_i\) and \(\vec{v}_j\) where \(i\) and \(j\) represent the indices of different proposals. And then, the idea quality is measured by:
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:idea_quality}
    \mathrm{IQ}_\mathrm{proposal} = \frac{1}{3}[\sum_{i=1}^K(M_0'[\vec{v}_i,]\ge 0) + \sum_{i=1}^K(M_0'[-\vec{v}_i,]\le 0) + \sum_{i=1}^K(\mid M_1'[+\vec{v}_i,]\mid + \mid M_1'[-\vec{v}_i,]\mid)],
\end{equation}
\textbf{Relevance and usefulness of criteria.}
First, the relevance of the criteria to each proposal is measured by the reward signal. We then calculate the 0-1 sparse vector \(s_i \) = [s$_1$, ..., $s_i, ..., s_K$] 
for each agent, where \(s_i\) is 1 if \(y^1_i = a^i_{\pi_\mathrm{AS}}\) or \(s_i = 1\) if $\pi_{\mathrm{AR}}$ or $\pi_{\mathrm{RA}}$ wins the final round, and 0 otherwise. 
Intuitively, we want the selected criteria to provide constructive and helpful feedback to improve and evolve ideas. We record an "evolution" of each proposal's quality over time, which is a sequence of preference datasets. Therefore, the relevance is measured by:
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:idea_evolve}
\mathrm{Re}_e = \frac{1}{K}(\sum_{i=1}^K(\vec{w_i}\cdot \vec{s_i}),
\end{equation}
where we consider the reward difference between proposals as temporal properties and represent them by a weight vector $\vec{w_i}$ from the reward signal. 
We also include the availability of the criteria into the evaluation metric, which is measured by the number of criteria each proposal associated with:
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:criteria_assign}
    \mathrm{Ca}_\mathrm{criteria} = \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^K \mid s_i \mid},
\end{equation}
\subsection{Role-Assigning Agent}
Given that some agents may lack memory of the previous exploration rounds, we have created two versions of the agent: an Epoch Memory Version and a Persistent Memory Version. 
The Epoch Memory Version is reset before each round of exploration, while the Persistent Memory Version maintains its memory across all iterations. To ensure that each version of the agent has a fair opportunity to learn from its opponent, we have developed an automated role-assigning mechanism that dynamically adjusts the roles of AS, RA, and AR throughout each iteration, ensuring that the Epoch Memory Version has more opportunities to learn from its opponent than the Persistent Memory Version. For example, during AS's exploration, Persistent AR or Persistent RA might be assigned to be the opponent of AS and then become the final winner. To maintain fairness, we allow the Epoch Memory agent to continuously explore the environment so that it may have more opportunities to win. In Section \ref{exp}, we show that the IMPO framework consistently improves the reward signal.

\subsection{Improving Agents via Fine-tuning}
We improve the three agents through fine-tuning and analyze how the proposed method conducts idea proposal, improvement and review during the exploration process. 
In the $k$-th episode, we first assign each agent with a specific role (AS, RA or AR) and initialize their states. 

\textbf{Action:} At time step $t$, given the current state of the environment, $s_t = (y^1, y^2, \pi_\mathrm{AS}, \pi_\mathrm{RA},\pi_\mathrm{AR})$, a stochastic agent, $\pi_\chi \sim \{\pi_\mathrm{AS}, \pi_\mathrm{RA},\pi_\mathrm{AR}\}$, parameterized by $\theta$, takes sample action $a_t$ from the current action distribution at current time-step $t$:
\begin{equation*}
    a_t = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t).  
\end{equation*}

\textbf{State transition:} After action $a_t$, a deterministic transition function $f$, which is determined by the environment itself, describes how the state evolves. In the environment of this paper, the state transition is determined by journal's and reviewer's acceptance or rejection of proposals and the assignment of roles given by the role assigning system:
\begin{equation*}
    s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t).  
\end{equation*}

\textbf{Reward signal:} Given a state of the environment, we define a reward signal $\phi$. The reward signal acts as a bridge between the environment state and the policy model. It provides feedback to the policy model, which then seeks to maximize the expected reward signal, representing the expected sum of rewards. The reward signal $\phi$ is determined by various factors, such as the relationship between agents, the quality of proposals, and the criteria used for reviews. In our experiments in the field of chemistry, a reward signal based on the quality criteria of proposals is used. Additional details and insights regarding the reward signal are provided in Section \ref{reward_signal}.


\textbf{Reward Model.} The reward model is trained on the preference dataset which is used in the preference optimization method \cite{rafailov2023direct}. At the beginning of the $n$-th iteration, the reward model is trained on \(\mathcal{D}_n^1, \mathcal{D}_n^2, ..., \mathcal{D}_n^K\), and is subsequently used to fine-tune the policy model.

\section{Experiments}

In this section, we present experiments to verify the following research questions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, noitemsep]
\item \textbf{RQ1:} How is the performance of the proposed method compared to the baseline methods and agent systems?
\item \textbf{RQ2:} How is the collaboration between agents?
\item \textbf{RQ3:} What are the effects of an iterative strategy and stochasticity?
\item \textbf{RQ4:} What is the knowledge evaluation of the agents?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{experiment setup}
Experiments on chemistry are quite few. Google has a rich patent database, the USPTO (US Patent and Trademark Office) dosier database \footnote{https://patents.google.com/}, containing grant applications from 1976 to the present, has been employed in prior works \cite{wang2023scimon}. We filtered dosier data from 2015 to 2023, removing self-references to compare criteria proposed by different policy models and ideas from different times. After filtering, 80 chemistry papers remained. We then randomly divided these papers into two subsets: 44 for training and 36 for evaluation.

\textbf{Implementation:} In the experiments, we choose low-rank adaption (LoRA) \cite{hu2022lora} to fine-tune from various base language models: GPT2, Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B, ChatGLM3-6B \cite{chatglm3}, and Qwen2.5 \cite{qwen2.5}. 
We train a reward model for each base language model.

\textbf{Evaluation Metrics:} We evaluated the output from our framework and the baselines in three aspects: total reward signal, idea quality, criteria relevance and usability.

\textbf{Total Reward Signal} We calculate the reward signal from the agent policy model and output the sum of the reward signals.

\textbf{Idea Quality} The idea quality is evaluated according to our defined metrics in Section \ref{feedback}. 

\textbf{Criteria Relevance and Usability} To measure the quality of reviews and the open-ended nature of review criteria, we use the reward signal to indicate the quality of the reviews. Additionally, we include criteria availability in the paper, defined as the average number of criteria assigned for each proposal. 

\textbf{Knowledge Evaluation} In addition to these evaluation methods, we also evaluate the knowledge parameters of agents and evaluate the coherence of the knowledge parameters of agents after fine-tuning. Specific metrics and metrics are shown in Section \ref{knowledge}.

\textbf{Output Knowledge Evaluation} To further evaluate the soundness of the proposed methods and the quality of the output knowledge, we calculate the total reward signal, criterion, and idea of the generated output.

The agent consistently enhances the quality of suggestions, making the most current proposal highly competitive. The high benefit score is attributed to the iterative optimization and AI agent collaboration process, which significantly enhances the criteria for proposing high-quality suggestions.

The criteria relevance is assessed by the following factors: whether the proposed idea aligns with the criteria and whether the criteria are relevant to evaluating the proposal. The table \ref{tab:criteria_relevance} shows that these criteria are highly relevant to the proposals, as evidenced by a relative relevance score of 1. Additionally, the criteria are widely applied to each proposal, supporting earlier findings of their broad applicability. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves the highest total reward signal. In contrast, the agent using fixed agent assignment and static iteration, SRGPT, achieves the lowest total reward signal, indicating the necessity of providing the agents with the ability to explore alternative proposals and iteratively optimize them.

\section{Conclusion}


In this study, we present evidence that our proposed agent is capable of acting more like human researchers, including generating and proposing new ideas, and providing critiques or evaluations of existing proposals. Through experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our agent in performing these tasks in the field of chemistry. Additionally, we provide evidence that our agent can be trained to produce outputs that meet specific criteria, and that the quality of these outputs can be improved through human feedback. Our research marks a step towards the development of intelligent machines capable of autonomous scientific research, which could expand human knowledge across various domains.

## Motivation

The field of AI-assisted scientific writing has seen significant advancements, but the lack of standardized benchmarks and rigorous evaluation protocols has hindered the objective assessment of these technologies. This gap in validation is particularly pronounced in the domain of scientific peer reviewing, a critical component of the scientific review process. The current methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted scientific writing methods, which often involves a single round of correction or modification, has shown limitations in terms of the models' ability to self-improve and the practicality of the benchmarks. Additionally, the reliability of LLM-generated text and their impact on trustworthiness in academic writing, especially in peer reviews, remain uncertain. Addressing these issues is crucial for advancing the field and ensuring that AI-assisted methods can be effectively leveraged to enhance scientific discovery. The paper aims to introduce a benchmark for LLM-assisted scientific writing that facilitates long-term, multi-round corrections and evaluations, and leverages these corrections to enhance the model's capabilities. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel approach to evaluate the reliability of LLM-augmented peer reviews by designing a robust and comprehensive dataset.

## Main Idea

The paper introduces WeWrite (Scientific Writing with Language Models), a framework that integrates multiple LLM-assisted writing methods into a comprehensive benchmark. The framework includes three primary methods: direct replacement, iterative refinement, and tool-assisted correction. Each method is designed to help researchers with different levels of expertise. The paper evaluates five LLMs in a simulated peer review environment and establishes a benchmark based on statistical significance, human preference, and reward scores. Additionally, the paper introduces AIP as an alternative LLM-assisting method and introduces SciPeer, a dataset tailored to assess the reliability of LLM-assisted peer reviews. The findings demonstrate that WeWrite enhances the performance of LLMs in scientific writing tasks, with specific models excelling in particular research genres. The paper also discusses ethical concerns and suggests solutions, such as agent-driven feedback during training, to address potential issues.

\title{Evaluating Language Models on Scientific Writing: Benchmarks, Algorithms, and Case Studies}

\begin{abstract}

Researchers have explored the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to scientific writing across various domains such as protein, chemistry, and materials. However, the lack of standardized benchmarks in this field has limited the objective evaluation of these technologies, making it challenging to quantify their impact on scientific discovery. 
To address this issue, we introduce a benchmark for scientific writing based on multi-round corrections from LLMs. 
In particular, our approach includes three primary methods to improve the writing ability of LLMs in three rounds: direct replacement, iterative refinement, and tool-assisted correction.
These methods are extensively evaluated on three scientific writing tasks across different levels of researcher expertise, including scientific writing, open review (peer review without anonymity), and multi-round review (a more rigorous and useful peer review process). 
Additionally, we explore Automatic Idea Proposal (AIP) as an alternative LLM-assisting method and introduce an innovative dataset, SciPeer, which is tailored to assess the reliability of LLM-assisted peer reviews. 
Our findings demonstrate that scientific writing can enhance the performance of LLMs on several benchmarks, with specific models excelling in particular research genres.
We also discuss ethical issues regarding fairness and bias, and suggest potential solutions like agent-driven feedback during the training process\end{abstract}

\label{sec: intro}
Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in transforming scientific research practices and significantly impacting the traditional process of scientific discovery~\cite{d2024marg,langley1987scientific,hayes2024simulating,ai4science2023impact,jumper2021highly,nuijten2016prevalence,pyzer2022accelerating,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can}. Applied in chemistry, materials, and physics, they have played pivotal ``cogents'' in addressing complex challenges with a degree of independence~\cite{dou2024marg,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,langley1987scientific,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,merchant2023scaling,liang2024can,wang2023scientific}. These techniques are also shown to help improve the understanding of real-world phenomena, such as the discovery of new mathematical problems~\cite{romera2024mathematical}, new scientific literature~\cite{langley2024integrated}, and new scientific topics~\cite{wang2023scimion,huang2024mlagentbench,yang2023large,li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning,baek2024researchagent}. They have been instrumental in elevating the efficiency and precision of large-scale experiments~\cite{hayes2024simulating,ai4science2023impact,jumper2021highly,nuijten2016prevalence,pyzer2022accelerating,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can,wang2023scientific}, as well as in generating synthetic data~\cite{dou2024marg,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can,wang2023scientific} and extracting knowledge from unstructured text~\cite{wang2024autosurvey}. These applications collectively underscore the versatility and positive impact of LLMs on the scientific community. Recently, LLM-assisted scientific writing based on prompting techniques has received considerable attention due to its practical application in peer review. A preliminary 
study suggests that LLM-assisted peer reviews can outperform the \textit{no correction} baseline in specific research domains, even for researchers with different levels of expertise~\cite{robertson2023gpt4}. However, the study has several limitations:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]

\item 
\textbf{The lack of long-term training limits the effectiveness of LLM-assisted writing methods:}
In the study, there is only one round of correction or modification for each tested sentence or paragraph. It remains unclear whether the model can self-improve by ``learning'' from its own modifications.

\item 
\textbf{The practicality of the benchmarks lacks long-term evaluation:}
In the study, the authors only study LLM-assisted writing in single-round open review. It remains an open question whether the method can be useful in a more challenging and useful peer review setting like multi-round review.
\item 
\textbf{The reliability of LLM-generated text and their impacts on peer reviews is uncertain:}
In the study, the reliability of LLM-generated text is not certain, especially considering that the model can modify text in infinite ways. 
It remains an open problem whether LLM-assisted writing will lead to reliable text in the long run.
\end{itemize}
To address the above issues, in this study, we propose a benchmark for LLM-assisted scientific writing based on statistical significance, human preference, and reward scores.
The benchmark includes three primary methods designed to assist researchers with different levels of expertise:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Direct Replacement:} it is the most straightforward method for assisting scientific writing. We prompt the LLM to replace the original text with a better modification.
\item \textit{Iterative Refinement:} it involves the LLM generating a draft in the first round and refining it in the second round, while keeping a set of semi-fixed original content from the draft.
\item \textit{Tool-assisted Correction:} it is the most efficient method and is especially suitable for researchers. We prompt the LLM to generate a draft and then to ``correct'' its own errors. We use the second round outputs to replace the corresponding first round output.
\end{itemize}
We evaluate the above methods in three peer review scenarios: open review and multi-round review. 
In open review, each paper is assigned three reviewers and the authors only know the scores assigned by each reviewer. In multi-round review, the authors can also see the scores from the first round and request for each reviewer to summarize their concerns in the second round. 
Multi-round review can improve the reliability of reviews and enhance the research artifacts' credibility~\cite{smith2006peer,boughton2018research,lu2024ai}.
By conducting pairwise human evaluations on the final LLM-generated text, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods in the above two peer review settings over \textit{no correction} baseline. We also provide ablation studies on each component in the methods and conduct replacement experiments to show that LLMs do not blindly replace text.
Additionally, we explore LLM-assisted writing from a different perspective: we propose \textit{Automatic Idea Proposal Generation} (AIP) to replace the ``Research Question'' section in the peer review reports. In peer review reports, the reviewer usually summarizes the questions to be addressed. We further transform these questions into five specific, measurable tasks and then use LLMs to generate possible answers to these questions. Our experiments demonstrate that proposed AIP can provide useful ideas in practice, with the potential to be combined with previous LLM-assisted writing methods.

Last but not least, we construct a new dataset, \textit{SciPeer}, to address the challenge of assessing the reliability of LLM-assisted scientific writing. The dataset includes peer reviews, peer review papers, and human annotations on the quality and biases of the reviews. The dataset comprises 110 papers and 305 corresponding peer review reports. We conduct comprehensive experiments using Qwen2.5-110B-Chat~\cite{qwen2.5}, GPT-3.5-turbo~\footnote{We first obtain the results on April 24, 2024.}~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, GPT-4o~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, GPT-4o-roberta~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2~\cite{jiang2023mistral}. Our experiments show that SciPeer poses a significant challenge for modern LLMs, highlighting the necessity of further advancements in developing robust and reliable LLM-assisted writing methods in the field of scientific writing.

This study focuses on creating and evaluating three LLM-assisted scientific writing algorithms, encompassing open review and multi-round review. Simultaneously, we explore the potential of alternative LLM-assisting scenarios and address the challenge of assessing reliability in LLM-assisted writing through a new peer review-oriented dataset, \textit{SciPeer}.


\section{Related Work}

\label{sec: related work}
The concept of automatically correcting and improving text has been an active area of research for decades~\cite{buchanan1981dendral,lenat1977automated,lenat1983eurisko,hutter2001towards,NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. This task is now attractivve because it is challenging and motivating~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. At the beginning, a series of algorithms are designed to automatically improve text~\cite{buchanan1981dendral,lenat1977automated,lenat1983eurisko,buchanan1981dendral}. Recently, with the rise of deep learning~\cite{Hinton06,goodfellow2016deep,Bengio+chapter2007}, especially the design of Transformer architecture in NLP~\cite{NIPS2017_3f5ee243}, we can mainly use sequence-to-sequence models to generate better text~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. Recently, this field has become a consensual topic with denoising task, because the challenge of this task is to balance the effectiveness and safety of the generated text. Recently, LLMs have demonstrated their remarkable performance~\cite{achiam2023gpt,reid2024gemini} in various NLP tasks, including denoising tasks such as peer reviewing in literature. 
In the literature, there are numerous algorithms for LLM-assisted scientific writing, including chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain}, self-verification~\cite{shinn2023reflexion,weng-etal-2023-large}, and other related algorithms~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview,tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext,liang2024mapping,zhang2024generative}. Among these various algorithms, chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain} is the most well-known and widely used due to its simplicity and high effectiveness. It is used in \textit{no modification} baseline and LLM-assisted writing methods in this study. In the following, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the related works with their limitations.
\textbf{Related works with limitations:}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{ReviewGPT~\cite{liu2023reviewergpt}}: it also proposes LLM-assisted writing methods in peer review scenarios. Compared to this study, we propose more advanced methods and conduct more extensive experiments on multi-round review. Additionally, we conduct experiments in several scientific writing genres and provide an ablation study on each component in our methods.
\item \textit{We Write Research Papers~\cite{hu2024automated}}: it is the first work to study LLM-assisted writing methods in scientific writing. This study is particularly significant as the first study, but our experiments show that its methods demonstrate limitations. Our work serves to complement and build upon its foundations.

\item \textit{A agentReview~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}}: it focuses on proposing and improving LLM-based reviewing agents. In contrast to our work, their work primarily studies how to (not) reduce the bias in LLMs in the review process. 
\item \textit{AutoReview~\cite{du2024llms}}: it focuses on exploring the advantages of using LLMs in the scientific writing process to assist researchers in engaging in peer review. We also leverage LLMs to assist peer reviewing in this study, but it remains unclear which methods are more efficient and suitable for researchers to assist in peer reviewing. 

\item \textit{Scideator~\cite{radensky2024scideator}}: it leverages LLMs to extract sentences and paragraphs from literature and then propose a novel scientific topic in high-level detail. The method can be used to assist in peer reviewing by providing high-level relevant literature. Our difference is that we leverage literature in a completely different way than the method.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Related works that focus on the advantages of leveraging LLM:} In the following, we explain the works that focus on the advantages of LLM-assisted writing in peer review:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{A agentReview~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview} }: it focuses on using reinforcement learning to improve the effectiveness of LLM-assisted writing in peer review. In our study, we utilize chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain} and other prompting techniques~\cite{hu2024automated} to guide the LLM in generating high-quality output via multi-round corrections instead of reinforcement learning.

\item \textit{AutoReview~\cite{du2024llms} }: it leverages LLMs to assist in scientific writing. However, in peer review scenarios, they only focus on a particular research domain called educational psychology without conducting multi-round reviews.

\item \textit{Scideator~\cite{radensky2024scideator}:} it proposes a method to ``read'' a large number of scientific literature, and then propose a high-level scientific topic that combines these literature. We use this method as one of the baselines to assist in peer reviewing.

\end{itemize}

\textbf{Related works on the evaluation of LLM-assisted writing methods:} There are no prior studies on evaluating LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing. In our study, we focus on the evaluation of LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing due to the following reasons:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{It is useful and challenging:} it is useful because we spend the most time on scientific writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. It is challenging because it requires a very high level of text quality~\cite{zhu2024locking}.
\item \textit{There are no available benchmarks:} In the field of LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing, benchmark construction remains an open problem with significant room for exploration. In the relevant field of educational research, \citet{oberg2022teaching} suggest that a well-organized benchmark can encourage the participation of a more diverse group of students. Following this perspective, we organize and design a peer review-oriented dataset. Additionally, we found that peer review data can naturally provide well-trained agents~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. These factors collectively suggest that peer review data can be naturally used to construct a benchmark in LLM-assisted writing.
\item \textit{There are no available standard approaches:} In peer review scenarios, there are various methods for evaluating the quality of language quality. For instance, in \cite{liu2023reviewergpt}, the authors use pass/fail rates to evaluate different methods in peer reviewing.
\end{itemize}



\section{Our Methods}

\label{sec: methods}
We provide an overview of our methods in Table~\ref{tab: methods}. The methods include three LLM-assisted writing methods in Table~\ref{tab: base methods}, with details on the algorithms in Table~\ref{tab: base}. These methods are especially designed to help researchers in different levels of expertise in particular:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Direct replacement:} It is designed to assist the most experienced group of researchers. We use direct replacement and iterative replacement in this method, as detailed in the third and fourth rows of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\item \textit{Iterative refinement:} It is designed to assist the middle group of researchers. We use iterative replacement in this method, as detailed in the second row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\item \textit{Tool-assisted correction:} It is designed to assist the least experienced group of researchers. We use iterative replacement and automatic correction in this method, as detailed in the second row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\end{itemize}

In addition, we introduce AIP (Automatic Idea Proposal) in this study, which is suitable for all three researcher groups. AIP involves LLMs generating answers to the questions (called ``Research Question'' in reports) for a single paper, as outlined in the fifth row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.

Each method is briefly introduced below, with the detailed algorithm in Table~\ref{tab: base}.

\textbf{Direct replacement:} 
We prompt the LLM to generate text for a given paragraph or section of text. We replace the original text with the newly generated text in the draft paper. 

\textbf{Iterative refinement:} From the original text, we extract keywords and ask the LLM to include these keywords in its generation. During the first round, the LLM generates draft text that serves as a rough modification. During the second round, we request the LLM to refine the draft by incorporating feedback based on generated ``review report''. We replace the original text in the draft paper with the second round output.

\textbf{Tool-assisted correction:} During the first round, the LLM generates a draft. During the second round, we request the LLM to correct these issues and produce the output. We replace the original text in the draft paper with the second round output.

\textbf{AIP:} We use LLMs to provide some interesting  ideas for a paper. For each paper, we extract sentences in five sections (Introduction, Related Work, Experimental, etc.) and then feed these sentences and the corresponding original paragraphs as well as other details (e.g., experimental setting for a experiment paper) into the LLM to get interesting ideas for each section. AIP is especially useful in practice because it is time-saving and reliable.

\section{Benchmark}

\label{sec: methods}
This section introduces the design of our benchmark in detail.

\textbf{Multi-round Review} \textbf{Scenario:} In addition to the single-round open review process in which each paper assigned to three reviewers as in~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}, in our benchmark, we conduct a multi-round review to assess whether the LLM method can help reviewers to summarize their concerns in the second round. In the first round of peer review, each paper assigned to three experienced reviewers, who read the paper and provide a score. Then, the reviewers review their own scores and correct the possible errors in their scores, as the first round scores. Finally, the authors submit their own paper and the scores from the reviewers. The authors read the scores and corresponding explanations from the reviewers and request each reviewer to either confirm or modify their own scoring and explanation. In multi-round review, we use Chain-of-Thought~\cite{wei2022chain} as the prompt for LLMs to generate the corresponding scores, explanations, and corrections.

\textbf{Dataset Construction:}
In scientific writing, a series of tasks are suitable for LLM-assisted writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. In our experiment, we focus (and will broaden in the future) on the peer review process because it is the most challenging and important task in scientific writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. In this study, we collect data from \citet{su2024analysisicml2023ranking} to construct the dataset for LLM-assisted writing experiments. We conduct ICML2023 paper-and-report retrieval and ICML2023 paper-and-revisions retrieval. We get 110 papers and corresponding 305 peer review reports. The data is summarized in Table~\ref{tab: dataset}. ICML2023 paper-and-report retrieval means that we retrieve the relevant peer review report for each paper. 
ICML2023 paper-revisions retrieval means that we retrieve all revisions for each paper.
This dataset can be used to test continuous improvement in LLM-assisted writing as well.

\textbf{Task Description:} In our experiments, we leverage the collected papers and data to evaluate the LLM-assisted writing methods. Following~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}, we assume that each LLM is an agent who is originally trained to engage in peer reviewing. In this study, we investigate whether the agents can help researchers improve their peer reviewing through the proposed LLM-assisted writing methods.

\textbf{Evaluation Metric:} In this study, we use three metrics to measure the quality of generation:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Statistical Significance~\cite{yang2024collaborative}:} It is the most important metric because it shows that the methods truly help researchers. To measure statistical significance, we use the ranking from the assistant (agent with LLM-assisted writing methods). We then conduct significant tests on the rankings, by comparing the rankings with the baseline rankings.
\item \textit{Human Preference~\cite{david1963method}:} It is the most intuitive metric because it reflects the quality of generation. In human preference evaluation, we hire a crowdsource worker to compare the LLM-generated content with the baseline generation.
\item \textit{Reward Model~\cite{lambert2024rewardbench}:} We use RewardBench~\cite{lambert2024rewardbench} to obtain the reward scores.
\end{itemize}

Researchers have explored the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to scientific writing across various domains such as protein, chemistry, and materials. To address this issue, we introduce a benchmark for scientific writing based on multi-round corrections from LLMs.

These methods are extensively evaluated on three scientific writing tasks across different levels of researcher expertise, including scientific writing, open review (peer review without anonymity), and multi-round review (a more rigorous and useful peer review process). 
Additionally, we explore Automatic Idea Proposal (AIP) as an alternative LLM-assisting method and introduce an innovative dataset, SciPeer, which is tailored to assess the reliability of LLM-assisted peer reviews.

\label{sec: intro}
Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in transforming scientific research practices and significantly impacting the traditional process of scientific discovery~\cite{d2024marg,langley1987scientific,hayes2024simulating,ai4science2023impact,jumper2021highly,nuijten2016prevalence,pyzer2022accelerating,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can}. Applied in chemistry, materials, and physics, they have played pivotal ``cogents'' in addressing complex challenges with a degree of independence~\cite{dou2024marg,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,langley1987scientific,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,merchant2023scaling,liang2024can,wang2023scientific}. These techniques are also shown to help improve the understanding of real-world phenomena, such as the discovery of new mathematical problems~\cite{romera2024mathematical}, new scientific literature~\cite{langley2024integrated}, and new scientific topics~\cite{wang2023scimion,huang2024mlagentbench,yang2023large,li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning,baek2024researchagent}. They have been instrumental in elevating the efficiency and precision of large-scale experiments~\cite{hayes2024simulating,ai4science2023impact,jumper2021highly,nuijten2016prevalence,pyzer2022accelerating,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can,wang2023scientific}, as well as in generating synthetic data~\cite{dou2024marg,ai4science2023impact,ai4science2023impact,reid2024gemini,achiam2023gpt,liang2024can,wang2023scientific} and extracting knowledge from unstructured text~\cite{wang2024autosurvey}. These applications collectively underscore the versatility and positive impact of LLMs on the scientific community. Recently, LLM-assisted scientific writing based on prompting techniques has received considerable attention due to its practical application in peer review. A preliminary 
study suggests that LLM-assisted peer reviews can outperform the \textit{no correction} baseline in specific research domains, even for researchers with different levels of expertise~\cite{robertson2023gpt4}. However, the study has several limitations:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]

\item 
\textbf{The lack of long-term training limits the effectiveness of LLM-assisted writing methods:}
In the study, there is only one round of correction or modification for each tested sentence or paragraph. It remains unclear whether the model can self-improve by ``learning'' from its own modifications.

\item 
\textbf{The practicality of the benchmarks lacks long-term evaluation:}
In the study, the authors only study LLM-assisted writing in single-round open review. It remains an open question whether the method can be useful in a more challenging and useful peer review setting like multi-round review.
\item 
\textbf{The reliability of LLM-generated text and their impacts on peer reviews is uncertain:}
In the study, the reliability of LLM-generated text is not certain, especially considering that the model can modify text in infinite ways. 
It remains an open problem whether LLM-assisted writing will lead to reliable text in the long run.
\end{itemize}
To address the above issues, in this study, we propose a benchmark for LLM-assisted scientific writing based on statistical significance, human preference, and reward scores.
The benchmark includes three primary methods designed to assist researchers with different levels of expertise:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Direct Replacement:} it is the most straightforward method for assisting scientific writing. We prompt the LLM to replace the original text with a better modification.
\item \textit{Iterative Refinement:} it involves the LLM generating a draft in the first round and refining it in the second round, while keeping a set of semi-fixed original content from the draft.
\item \textit{Tool-assisted Correction:} it is the most efficient method and is especially suitable for researchers. We prompt the LLM to generate a draft and then to ``correct'' its own errors. We use the second round outputs to replace the corresponding first round output.
\end{itemize}
We evaluate the above methods in three peer review scenarios: open review and multi-round review. 
In open review, each paper is assigned three reviewers and the authors only know the scores assigned by each reviewer. In multi-round review, the authors can also see the scores from the first round and request for each reviewer to summarize their concerns in the second round. 
Multi-round review can improve the reliability of reviews and enhance the research artifacts' credibility~\cite{smith2006peer,boughton2018research,lu2024ai}.
By conducting pairwise human evaluations on the final LLM-generated text, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods in the above two peer review settings over \textit{no correction} baseline. We also provide ablation studies on each component in the methods and conduct replacement experiments to show that LLMs do not blindly replace text.
Additionally, we explore LLM-assisted writing from a different perspective: we propose \textit{Automatic Idea Proposal Generation} (AIP) to replace the ``Research Question'' section in the peer review reports. In peer review reports, the reviewer usually summarizes the questions to be addressed. We further transform these questions into five specific, measurable tasks and then use LLMs to generate possible answers to these questions. Our experiments demonstrate that proposed AIP can provide useful ideas in practice, with the potential to be combined with previous LLM-assisted writing methods.

Last but not least, we construct a new dataset, \textit{SciPeer}, to address the challenge of assessing the reliability of LLM-assisted scientific writing. The dataset includes peer reviews, peer review papers, and human annotations on the quality and biases of the reviews. The dataset comprises 110 papers and 305 corresponding peer review reports. We conduct comprehensive experiments using Qwen2.5-110B-Chat~\cite{qwen2.5}, GPT-3.5-turbo~\footnote{We first obtain the results on April 24, 2024.}~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, GPT-4o~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, GPT-4o-roberta~\cite{achiam2023gpt}, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2~\cite{jiang2023mistral}. Our experiments show that SciPeer poses a significant challenge for modern LLMs, highlighting the necessity of further advancements in developing robust and reliable LLM-assisted writing methods in the field of scientific writing.

This study focuses on creating and evaluating three LLM-assisted scientific writing algorithms, encompassing open review and multi-round review. Simultaneously, we explore the potential of alternative LLM-assisting scenarios and address the challenge of assessing reliability in LLM-assisted writing through a new peer review-oriented dataset, \textit{SciPeer}.


\section{Related Work}

\label{sec: related work}
The concept of automatically correcting and improving text has been an active area of research for decades~\cite{buchanan1981dendral,lenat1977automated,lenat1983eurisko,hutter2001towards,NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. This task is now attractivve because it is challenging and motivating~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. At the beginning, a series of algorithms are designed to automatically improve text~\cite{buchanan1981dendral,lenat1977automated,lenat1983eurisko,buchanan1981dendral}. Recently, with the rise of deep learning~\cite{Hinton06,goodfellow2016deep,Bengio+chapter2007}, especially the design of Transformer architecture in NLP~\cite{NIPS2017_3f5ee243}, we can mainly use sequence-to-sequence models to generate better text~\cite{NEURIPS2020_6b493230}. Recently, this field has become a consensual topic with denoising task, because the challenge of this task is to balance the effectiveness and safety of the generated text. Recently, LLMs have demonstrated their remarkable performance~\cite{achiam2023gpt,reid2024gemini} in various NLP tasks, including denoising tasks such as peer reviewing in literature. 
In the literature, there are numerous algorithms for LLM-assisted scientific writing, including chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain}, self-verification~\cite{shinn2023reflexion,weng-etal-2023-large}, and other related algorithms~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview,tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext,liang2024mapping,zhang2024generative}. Among these various algorithms, chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain} is the most well-known and widely used due to its simplicity and high effectiveness. It is used in \textit{no modification} baseline and LLM-assisted writing methods in this study. In the following, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the related works with their limitations.
\textbf{Related works with limitations:}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{ReviewGPT~\cite{liu2023reviewergpt}}: it also proposes LLM-assisted writing methods in peer review scenarios. Compared to this study, we propose more advanced methods and conduct more extensive experiments on multi-round review. Additionally, we conduct experiments in several scientific writing genres and provide an ablation study on each component in our methods.
\item \textit{We Write Research Papers~\cite{hu2024automated}}: it is the first work to study LLM-assisted writing methods in scientific writing. This study is particularly significant as the first study, but our experiments show that its methods demonstrate limitations. Our work serves to complement and build upon its foundations.

\item \textit{A agentReview~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}}: it focuses on proposing and improving LLM-based reviewing agents. In contrast to our work, their work primarily studies how to (not) reduce the bias in LLMs in the review process. 
\item \textit{AutoReview~\cite{du2024llms}}: it focuses on exploring the advantages of using LLMs in the scientific writing process to assist researchers in engaging in peer review. We also leverage LLMs to assist peer reviewing in this study, but it remains unclear which methods are more efficient and suitable for researchers to assist in peer reviewing. 

\item \textit{Scideator~\cite{radensky2024scideator}}: it leverages LLMs to extract sentences and paragraphs from literature and then propose a novel scientific topic in high-level detail. The method can be used to assist in peer reviewing by providing high-level relevant literature. Our difference is that we leverage literature in a completely different way than the method.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Related works that focus on the advantages of leveraging LLM:} In the following, we explain the works that focus on the advantages of LLM-assisted writing in peer review:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{A agentReview~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview} }: it focuses on using reinforcement learning to improve the effectiveness of LLM-assisted writing in peer review. In our study, we utilize chain-of-thought~\cite{wei2022chain} and other prompting techniques~\cite{hu2024automated} to guide the LLM in generating high-quality output via multi-round corrections instead of reinforcement learning.

\item \textit{AutoReview~\cite{du2024llms} }: it leverages LLMs to assist in scientific writing. However, in peer review scenarios, they only focus on a particular research domain called educational psychology without conducting multi-round reviews.

\item \textit{Scideator~\cite{radensky2024scideator}:} it proposes a method to ``read'' a large number of scientific literature, and then propose a high-level scientific topic that combines these literature. We use this method as one of the baselines to assist in peer reviewing.

\end{itemize}

\textbf{Related works on the evaluation of LLM-assisted writing methods:} There are no prior studies on evaluating LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing. In our study, we focus on the evaluation of LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing due to the following reasons:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{It is useful and challenging:} it is useful because we spend the most time on scientific writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. It is challenging because it requires a very high level of text quality~\cite{zhu2024locking}.
\item \textit{There are no available benchmarks:} In the field of LLM-assisted writing in scientific writing, benchmark construction remains an open problem with significant room for exploration. In the relevant field of educational research, \citet{oberg2022teaching} suggest that a well-organized benchmark can encourage the participation of a more diverse group of students. Following this perspective, we organize and design a peer review-oriented dataset. Additionally, we found that peer review data can naturally provide well-trained agents~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. These factors collectively suggest that peer review data can be naturally used to construct a benchmark in LLM-assisted writing.
\item \textit{There are no available standard approaches:} In peer review scenarios, there are various methods for evaluating the quality of language quality. For instance, in \cite{liu2023reviewergpt}, the authors use pass/fail rates to evaluate different methods in peer reviewing.
\end{itemize}



\section{Our Methods}

\label{sec: methods}
We provide an overview of our methods in Table~\ref{tab: methods}. The methods include three LLM-assisted writing methods in Table~\ref{tab: base methods}, with details on the algorithms in Table~\ref{tab: base}. These methods are especially designed to help researchers in different levels of expertise in particular:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Direct replacement:} It is designed to assist the most experienced group of researchers. We use direct replacement and iterative replacement in this method, as detailed in the third and fourth rows of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\item \textit{Iterative refinement:} It is designed to assist the middle group of researchers. We use iterative replacement in this method, as detailed in the second row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\item \textit{Tool-assisted correction:} It is designed to assist the least experienced group of researchers. We use iterative replacement and automatic correction in this method, as detailed in the second row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.
\end{itemize}

In addition, we introduce AIP (Automatic Idea Proposal) in this study, which is suitable for all three researcher groups. AIP involves LLMs generating answers to the questions (called ``Research Question'' in reports) for a single paper, as outlined in the fifth row of Table~\ref{tab: base methods}.

Each method is briefly introduced below, with the detailed algorithm in Table~\ref{tab: base}.

\textbf{Direct replacement:} 
We prompt the LLM to generate text for a given paragraph or section of text. We replace the original text with the newly generated text in the draft paper. 

\textbf{Iterative refinement:} From the original text, we extract keywords and ask the LLM to include these keywords in its generation. During the first round, the LLM generates draft text that serves as a rough modification. During the second round, we request the LLM to refine the draft by incorporating feedback based on generated ``review report''. We replace the original text in the draft paper with the second round output.

\textbf{Tool-assisted correction:} During the first round, the LLM generates a draft. During the second round, we request the LLM to correct these issues and produce the output. We replace the original text in the draft paper with the second round output.

\textbf{AIP:} We use LLMs to provide some interesting  ideas for a paper. For each paper, we extract sentences in five sections (Introduction, Related Work, Experimental, etc.) and then feed these sentences and the corresponding original paragraphs as well as other details (e.g., experimental setting for a experiment paper) into the LLM to get interesting ideas for each section. AIP is especially useful in practice because it is time-saving and reliable.

\section{Benchmark}

\label{sec: methods}
This section introduces the design of our benchmark in detail.

\textbf{Multi-round Review} \textbf{Scenario:} In addition to the single-round open review process in which each paper assigned to three reviewers as in~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}, in our benchmark, we conduct a multi-round review to assess whether the LLM method can help reviewers to summarize their concerns in the second round. In the first round of peer review, each paper assigned to three experienced reviewers, who read the paper and provide a score. Then, the reviewers review their own scores and correct the possible errors in their scores, as the first round scores. Finally, the authors submit their own paper and the scores from the reviewers. The authors read the scores and corresponding explanations from the reviewers and request each reviewer to either confirm or modify their own scoring and explanation. In multi-round review, we use Chain-of-Thought~\cite{wei2022chain} as the prompt for LLMs to generate the corresponding scores, explanations, and corrections.

\textbf{Dataset Construction:}
In scientific writing, a series of tasks are suitable for LLM-assisted writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. In our experiment, we focus (and will broaden in the future) on the peer review process because it is the most challenging and important task in scientific writing~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}. In this study, we collect data from \citet{su2024analysisicml2023ranking} to construct the dataset for LLM-assisted writing experiments. We conduct ICML2023 paper-and-report retrieval and ICML2023 paper-and-revisions retrieval. We get 110 papers and corresponding 305 peer review reports. The data is summarized in Table~\ref{tab: dataset}. ICML2023 paper-and-report retrieval means that we retrieve the relevant peer review report for each paper. 
ICML2023 paper-revisions retrieval means that we retrieve all revisions for each paper.
This dataset can be used to test continuous improvement in LLM-assisted writing as well.

\textbf{Task Description:} In our experiments, we leverage the collected papers and data to evaluate the LLM-assisted writing methods. Following~\cite{jin2024agentreviewexploringpeerreview}, we assume that each LLM is an agent who is originally trained to engage in peer reviewing. In this study, we investigate whether the agents can help researchers improve their peer reviewing through the proposed LLM-assisted writing methods.

\textbf{Evaluation Metric:} In this study, we use three metrics to measure the quality of generation:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item \textit{Statistical Significance~\cite{yang2024collaborative}:} It is the most important metric because it shows that the methods truly help researchers. To measure statistical significance, we use the ranking from the assistant (agent with LLM-assisted writing methods). We then conduct significant tests on the rankings, by comparing the rankings with the baseline rankings.
\item \textit{Human Preference~\cite{david1963method}:} It is the most intuitive metric because it reflects the quality of generation. In human preference evaluation, we hire a crowdsource worker to compare the LLM-generated content with the baseline generation.
\item \textit{Reward Model~\cite{lambert2024rewardbench}:} We use RewardBench~\cite{lambert2024rewardbench} to obtain the reward scores.
\end{itemize}
