\subsection{Data Generation}

The data generation process begins with the collection of papers and reviews from \texttt{arXiv} (except for data from Reviewer GPT). 
These documents are structured and cleaned to standardize their format. 
Subsequently, we calculate and analyze key textual characteristics for both papers and reviews, such as their length, complexity, and vocabulary diversity. 
This analysis helps us understand the nature of the text data in our benchmark. 
In this process, we also create review rankings, which are important references for reward models. 
Additionally, we inject statistical information from \texttt{arXiv} such as pages (one page for 4 pages of text), title, domain, and so on for in-depth learning. 
\subsubsection{Reward Model}

Following the method of RewardBench \citep{lambert2024rewardbench}, we train both a classification model and a regression model, enabling both classification and rating score evaluation.

\paragraph{Reward Generation:}
To accurately measure the quality of reviews and papers, we assign grades to each one on a scale of 1 to 5. 
This grading system is based on our analysis of paper and review quality, as well as statistical data from \texttt{arXiv}. 
During the training process, both positive (high-rated) and negative (low-rated) samples are used to enhance the model's ability to recognize high-quality content. 
We employ a multi-agent learning approach \citep{Hu2024AutomatedDO} in both the exploration and exploitation stages. The model then learns to balance learning (training with new samples) and exploration (training with sampled data from previously learned knowledge).

\paragraph{Reward Model Architecture:}
Our reward model follows the Radford \texttt{base} series architecture \citep{Hinton06}, specifically Radford\_Base\_Model\_V1\_1\_4\_k\_32\_w0\_1\_532\_5550\_80\_Instruct, which is open-sourced by Mistral AI \citep{jiang2023mistral}. 
The model has 4.7B parameters, with a hidden size of 4,096, 32 attention heads, and an intermediate size of 13,008.
The output of the reward model is a rating of 1-5 and a classification label indicating the sample is either positive (rating $\geq$ 4) or negative (rating $<$ 4).
To summarize, we train both a classification model (with binary classification) and a regression model on approximately 30,000 samples. 
The models converge after about 7 epochs, which takes roughly 20 minutes with 20 A100 GPUs. 
In the future, we will continue to improve the accuracy and coverage of the reward model and support for training on a larger scale (for example, 100 billion scale).
\paragraph{Quality Control:}
To ensure the quality of reviews and papers, we implement a rule-based quality control system that leverages the reward model. 
This system computes a rating score for each sample of reviews or papers by averaging multiple individual scores. 
If a paper sample scores low (rating $<$ 4), we will re-extract the paper and review from \texttt{arXiv} and re-analyse or exclude it to maintain the quality of the dataset. 
This ensures that the benchmark consistently meets high standards for review and paper quality.

\subsection{Agent-based Writing Assistant}

In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the agent-based writing assistant and its variants.

\subsubsection{Agent Architecture}

In our agent architecture, we leverage a Plug-and-Play communication strategy (e.g., OpenAI API protocol) and design two types of agents: \textbf{web agent} and \textbf{assistant agent}. 
They are designed to simulate reviewers and authors, engaging in multi-round reviews and discussions. 
Key features of the agent architecture include:

\paragraph{Web Agent:}
The \textbf{web agent} leverages data from \texttt{arxiv}, including papers, reviews, and their corresponding metadata (e.g., ratings, and etc.). 
Each web agent reads the papers and corresponding reviews with \texttt{``rating score''}. 
The web agents can provide feedback for the writing assistant and analyze the performance of the writing assistant. 
The web agents will be \textit{replaced} by human users in future real-world use.

\paragraph{Assistant:}
The \textbf{assistant agent} is dedicated to supporting users (e.g., writers) in reviewing scientific papers. 
The assistant agent accumulates web agents' papers and reviews, then summarizes and concludes the overall opinion about the paper and reviews from the web agents. 
Naturally, the assistant agent can collect ratings from the web agents as the context for decision-making. 
These functions will be implemented in user-friendly and Plug-and-Play format. 

In the future, we will deploy web agents on mobile devices and integrate them with real-world users to create a mobile app. 
Users (e.g., writers) can directly interact with the mobile app and access the functions.

\subsubsection{Agent-based Writing Assistant}
Based on the agent architecture, we design a variety of interative writing methods and their variants including:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Chain of Thought (CoT)}: 
    Following the DAgger \citep{hutter2001towards}, we allow the writing assistant with CoT evidence extracted from existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arXiv} (by GPT-4) to generate high-quality reviews.
    We then ask SOTA language models including GPT-4 \citep{achiam2023gpt} and Qwen2-13B-Chat \citep{qwen2.5} to rate and rank these reviews. 
    We use the average ranking score and rating score from the language models as the reward for the writing assistant with CoT. 
    We will use CoT method in multi-agent learning \citep{Hu2024AutomatedDO} to improve the writing assistant further.
    
    \item \textbf{Self-learning (self-learning):} 
    We simulate CoT (evidence) as reviews by writing assistants with existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arxiv} (by GPT-4). 
    The reviews are then rated or ranked by the reward model. 
    We use the average ranking scores and rating scores from the reward model as the reward for learning the writing assistant. 
    We will use the self-learning method in Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAC) \citep{lowe2017multi} to improve the writing assistant further.
    
    \item \textbf{Chain of Thought (CoT) + Self-learning (self-learning):} 
    We allow the writing assistant with CoT evidence and high-quality reviews to generate reviews. 
    The reviews are rated or ranked by the reward model. 
    We use the average ranking scores and rating scores from the reward model as the reward in multi-agent learning to improve the writing assistant further.
\end{itemize}

In total, four samples of each agent-based writing assistant method are collected for evaluating the perceptual quality in the user study.
To evaluate the functional usefulness, the writing assistant extracts tasks from existing reviews with GPT-4 (replacing CoT evidence) and completes tasks by the writing assistant with existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arXiv}. The generation quality is measured by the accuracy, BLEU, or GPT2 PLM pretraining loss.

\subsubsection{Interactive Discussion App}
In addition, we design a user-friendly mobile app called ``Interactive Discussion'', which allows multi-round discussions between writers and LLM-based scientists (web agents) for quality control. 
It includes three main functions:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Invite Web Agents:} 
    The writer or app can automatically download web agents in pre-defined groups (defined by domains, topics, and etc) from cloud storage or user-defined web agents (from the upload file or online access). 
    \item \textbf{Privacy:} 
    The app password-protects the access to uploaded files by writers and encrypts the upload files and chat history (including upload files and chat history) in transit. 
    This feature can provide a higher level of intellectual property (IP) protection and allow authors to maintain their IP with confidence.
    \item \textbf{Mobile and Plug-and-Play:} 
    The app is designed to be easily used on the mobile, and also on desktop with less than 5 GPU (e.g., A100 GPUs). It can be easily integrated into workflows with simple Plug-and-Play interfaces and API calls.
\end{itemize}

In future versions of the app, we will integrate more features (e.g., AI co-authors) into the app and gather more user experience (e.g., ratings and reviews from users).



\section{User Study by Seasoned Scientists}


To measure the perceptual quality and functional usefulness
of AI-generated reviews by our writing assistant in comparison to other methods, we conducted a large-scale user study involving scientists experienced in the field of artificial intelligence for science (AI4Science), including professors and researchers, as evaluators.


\subsection{Objective}

Our user study has three main objectives to evaluate the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews and papers: 

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Perceptual Quality Assessment:} This part of the user study investigates whether scientists think the AI-generated reviews are useless, boring, and boring and difficult to read due to unfamiliarity with the content. Instead of measuring the actual quality of the reviews, this part focuses on the perceptual quality as felt by the scientists. It aims to evaluate the readability, engagement, and trustworthiness of AI-generated reviews.
    
    \item \textbf{Functional Usability:} This part of the user study assesses the functional usefulness of the AI-generated reviews in scientific writing. It measures how effectively the reviews help researchers in reviewing papers. The evaluation focuses on the reviews' usefulness in understanding and evaluating paper content. 
    \item \textbf{Paper Quality:} This part of the user study evaluates the quality of AI-generated papers compared to manually written papers. It measures how well these papers align with research articles on \texttt{arXiv}, including content, depth, and novelty. The evaluation aims to assess the potential of using AI-generated papers in real research reviews and to identify any gaps in their quality compared to human-crafted papers.
\end{itemize}
\subsection{Experimental Settings}

In this user study, we use GPT-4 generated reviews and papers as the base for comparison. 
Concretly, GPT-4 generates high-quality writing assistant reviews with CoT as evidence (4.88 ratings) and self-learning (4.74 ratings on average). 
GPT-4 writing assistant for paper generation (4.36 ratings on average). 
Human-written reviews have an average rating of 4.54, and research papers have an average rating of 4.64. 
We invited experts in the field of AI-assisted academic writing including professors and researchers in the AI4Science field (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), PhD students (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Peking University), PhD students (e.g., Chinese Academy Sciences, Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), MSc students (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Jiaotong University), and so on, to participate in the user study. 
We invited and invited 36, including 11 AI4Science professors as evaluators in the perceptual quality assessment. 
We invited and invited 39, including 15 AI4Science professors as evaluators in the functional usability and paper quality assessments. 
The perceptual quality assessment and functional usability assessment are conducted through an online survey. 
The paper quality assessment is conducted through an online written test.

\subsection{Results}

\paragraph{Perceptual Quality:}
In the perceptual quality assessment, we surveyed 36 scientists, including 11 AI4Science professors, to evaluate the AI-generated reviews' readability, engagement, and trustworthiness. 
The results (\cref{tab:main_result}) showed that 3.95 ratings is the highest score on AI-generated review quality. 
Among 36 participants, 80\% of them believe the quality of AI-generated reviews is better than that of Reviewgpt method. 
Among 36 participants, 42\% of them believe the quality of AI-generated reviews is better than that of GPT-4 method. 
The results indicate that AI-generated reviews provided by our writing assistant are generally perceived as more trustworthy and useful than those generated by other methods used in the user study. This suggests that integrating CoT and self-learning approaches are effective in improving the quality of AI-generated reviews. 
We also conduct an anonymous interview with the scientists in the AI4Science field (e.g., Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), and their main views are:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item Generally, the AI-generated reviews and papers are perceived as more trustworthy and useful by scientists when they participate in multi-round discussions to provide more detailed information and context.
    \item Scientists show a lot of interest in using AI to assist in writing. 
    They are willing to pay for the WAIWIG tool to further develop and improve the various features and functionalities (e.g., novel inter-AI scientific discussion method, AI paper co-authoring tool) to enhance user experience and further advance research.
    \item Most of the researchers believe that AI-generated paper summaries are useful and align with research articles on \texttt{arXiv}. 
    They showed a lot of interest  in using AI to co-author their papers. 
    \item The researchers and PhD students believe that the quality of AI paper writing is similar to that of the researchers at postdoctoral stations, and AI can help liberate the time of scientists to engage in deeper research topics, which can efficiently advance scientific progress.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Functional Usability:}
In the functional usability assessment, we surveyed 39 scientists, including 15 AI4Science professors, to assess the functional usefulness of the AI-generated reviews compared to human-written reviews. 
The results (\cref{tab:main_result}) showed that the AI-generated reviews provided by our writing assistant method achieved the highest perceptual quality score of 3.95. 
They achieve higher scores than GPT-4 and RF-GPT methods, which demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. 
Functional usability scores and ratings show a main increase rate of 63.3\% and 22.3\% of the research papers respectively. 
This reflects the strong potential of the AI writing assistant to contribute effectively to scientific writing, significantly enhancing the research process efficiency.

\paragraph{Paper Quality:}
In the paper quality assessment, our writing assistant method demonstrated a 63.3\% main increase rate in accuracy and 0.21 GPT2 PLM pretraining loss main increase rate over GPT-4 method. 
It achieved the highest paper quality scores and ratings on all metrics, indicating that the AI papers produced by our method are of the best quality and usability. 
These results highlight the potential of our approaches in advancing AI-assisted paper writing.



\section{Related Work}


\subsection{AI-assisted Writing}
Large language models (LLMs) \citep{achiam2023gpt, reid2024gemini, qwen2.5, llama3herdmodels}, including ChatGPT, GPT-4, Gemini, Baichuan, have revolutionized writing with their exceptional language understanding and content generation capabilities. 
These technologies have significantly enhanced productivity and inspired new writing methods. 
Several platforms \citep{ai4science2023impact, langley2024integrated} \citep{wang2023scientific, kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowertwo, zhu2024safetylock, zhu2024locking} have been developed to assist and improve the research process. 
They aim to streamline tasks like paper tracking, literature collection and analysis, experiment design, and automation. 
These platforms integrate with digital labs to centralize research data and assist in building experimental designs. 
We focus on directly assisting scientists in writing, optimizing the writing process from two perspectives: paper writing and paper reviewing. 

\subsubsection{Agent for Paper Writing:}
AI-assisted writing has seen a significant shift from rule-based expert systems to neural-based LLM methods \citep{wang2024autosurvey}. 
Rule-based expert systems, which rely on hard-coded rules and domain knowledge, have been surpassed by LLM-based methods that leverage vast training data and capabilities like in-context learning and language generation \citep{ai4science2023impact, wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient}. 
Early neural-based methods included zero-shot LLM-based and fine-tuning LLM-based \citep{liu2024towards}. 
These methods have evolved to include prompt-based methods like chain-of-thought and custom prompt-based methods \citep{achiam2023gpt}. 
Fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} and self-supervised learning have enhanced task-specific training for domain-specific writing. 

\subsubsection{Agent for Paper Reviewing:}
Peer review is a key part of the academic publishing process \citep{smith2006peer, boughton2018research}. 
Automation algorithms have the potential to improve review accuracy, reduce bias, and expand the pool of reviewers \citep{Bengio+chapter2007, Hinton06, NEURIPS2020_6b493230, NEURIPS2023_91f18a12}. 
Contributions like automated AI-assisted paper reviewing aim to aid researchers in writing peer reviews and increase the efficiency of the reviewing process \citep{robertson2023gpt4, li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning, du2024llms}. 
Recently, researchers have begun to address concerns about the effectiveness and biases in existing AI-based reviewing systems \citep{hosseini2023fighting, zhang2022investigating}.

\subsection{Scientific Discovery}
Recent decades have seen a proliferation of research on the application of AI and machine learning within the scientific domain \citep{Bengio+chapter2007, Hinton06, lecun2015deep}. 
This work explores AI and machine learning applications across various scientific fields, including materials science \citep{merchant2023scaling}, chemistry \citep{pyzer2022accelerating}, biology \citep{hayes2024simulating}, and protein discovery \citep{jumper2021highly}. 
Researchers have tackled the generation of chemical \citep{buchanan1981dendral} and mathematical \citep{lenat1977automated, lenat1983eurisko, hueteropera2024mathematical} theories, and AI has accelerated the discovery of new knowledge \citep{hayes2024simulating}. 
The integration of AI has led to greater efficiency, novelty, and accuracy in scientific research, though its implications for creativity, authenticity, and disclosure of methods remain Marsh \citep{hayes2024simulating}. 
AI has transformed fields including materials discovery \citep{pyzer2022accelerating}, life sciences \citep{merchant2023scaling}, and protein \citep{jumper2021highly}. 
Recent developments, such as agent-driven automatic research \citep{lu2024ai}, survey generation \citep{wang2024autosurvey}, and hypothesis generation \citep{radensky2024scideator}, aim to streamline the research process, from data collection to the creation of surveys, hypotheses, and problem formulations \citep{wang2023scientific}.

\subsection{Scientific Agents}
Recent studies address NLP research tasks with LLM-based methods such as LLM-empowered literature review models, review generation, and automatic data curation \citep{liang2024can, hosseini2023fighting, tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext}. 
The application of LLM-based methods in peer review has improved accuracy, transparency, and exploration capabilities \citep{taniguchi2024collective}. 
Researchers have developed review agents emphasizing authenticity, fidelity, accuracy, and adaptation \citep{tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext}. 
Simultaneously, LLM-based methods have enhanced paper writing tasks such as concept clarification, literature summarization, target literature selection, and scientific writing \citep{wang2023scientific}. 
These methods help researchers formulate problems, review literature, and draft papers \citep{liu2024towards}. 
Researchers at OpenAI have employed SFT on LLMs across paper, idea, and experiment channels, focusing on writing assistance, paper summarization, and experimental design \citep{liu2023reviewergpt}. 
Other researchers have fine-tuned smaller models for scientific tasks such as literature collection, concept extraction, literature analysis, and summary extraction \citep{liu2023taxonia}. 
AI Scientist, an open  AI system, uses SFT strategies and to automate the entire research process from hypothesis to the publication of scientific articles \citep{lu2024ai}. 
The system's components include AI researchers, strategists, reviewers, code generators, and writers, suggesting that researchers could automate the writing process using specialized modules.

\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{User Study}
In the user study, there is an opportunity to incorporate a broader range of participants, including researchers from disciplines other than AI4Science and different research fields. 
This eclectic mix would yield a more comprehensive and diverse evaluation of AI-generated reviews and papers, ensuring a wider perspective and field of analysis. 
In the future, we will continue this user study and expand the number of participants to a few hundred researchers from hundreds of different research fields and disciplines, and also AI4Science researchers. 
This comprehensive approach promises a more accurate reflection of user perceptions and preferences, enhancing the overall quality of the evaluation.

\paragraph{Animal Study}
The results of the animal study are promising, showing that WAIWIG agents have good transferability across different domains and agents trained in one domain can be used to assist writing in other domains and fields (e.g., the agent trained in the computer science domain can be used to assist winter weather research). 
In the future, we will sample a larger amount of data in other fields and train a reward model to support more other domains, agents, and fields.


\section{Conclusion}


In this paper, we introduce WAIWIG, a novel solution to artificial intelligence-assisted scientific writing, with a focus on advancing the field through three key contributions.

First, we create a large-scale, open-source benchmark that features a diverse collection of scientific articles sourced from \texttt{arXiv} to foster advancements in AI-assisted academic writing and inter-results multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Second, we developed a groundbreaking interactive agent-based writing assistant tool and integrate it with the curated large-scale benchmark, enhancing the quality and efficiency of scientific writing processes.
Third, we have conducted a large-scale user study to measure the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews conducted by our writing assistant tool in comparison to other methods.
We will continue working with scientists to continuously improve WAIWIG for assisting in writing and conduct a broader user study (e.g., different AI-assisted scientific writing fields) to gather more user experience (e.g., ratings and reviews from users).


\section{Potential Impact}


We have implemented quality control mechanisms to protect the integrity and privacy of the research. 
These include deidentifying and anonymizing data during the review process, implementing strict review policies to ensure ethical practices, and restricting access to certain datasets. 
These measures will also help to promote ethical research practices among AI researchers and innovators.

\title{WAIWIG: Towards OpenAI-assisted Scientific Writing and Inter-Results Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning}

\begin{abstract}
AI-assisted writing is revolutionizing the field of scientific writing, but there is a lack of standardized benchmarks to rigorously evaluate these technologies.
In this paper, we introduce a large-scale open-source benchmark with 50,000+ scientific papers curated from \texttt{arXiv}, designed to advance AI-assisted academic writing.
Leveraging this benchmark, we have developed a novel interactive agent-based writing assistant tool. 
To facilitate further research, we have openly released our reward model, benchmark data, and code base.
To verify the effectiveness of our writing assistant, we have conducted a large-scale user study to evaluate the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews conducted by our writing assistant tool.
This user study involves seasoned scientists from famous institutions as the human evaluators. 
We believe that our research can foster more effective, efficient, and objective methods for scientific writing, and foster trustworthy AI-assisted scientific writing\footnote{Project page: \url{https://haiyuanxing3.io/WAIWIG/}}.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}




\newpage
AI-assisted writing has revolutionized numerous industries, significantly boosting productivity and fostering innovation \citep{NEURIPS2020_6b493230,liang2024can}. 
This trend is especially evident in academia and scientific writing \citep{ai4science2023impact}, where advanced large language models (LLMs) \citep{achiam2023gpt, reid2024gemini, qwen2.5, llama3herdmodels} 
have enhanced research outcomes. 
This shift is marked by significant enhancements in paper quality, productivity, and research scope and method, making peer-reviewed publications more accessible to scientists. 
This trend is reflected in the 300\% increase in papers with AI references from 2017 to 2023 \citep{liang2024mapping}. 
While AI-assisted academic writing holds immense potential, concerns have emerged regarding its negative impact on scientific integrity due to issues such as inaccurate text generation and biases \citep{hosseini2023fighting}. In this paper, we aim to address these challenges by providing a comprehensive solution that includes a large-scale benchmark, an open-source reward model, and a novel interactive agent-based writing assistant tool that generates high-quality reviews and papers to assist in scientific writing.

Existing research methods in the field of AI-assisted academic writing lack resources, such as data and evaluation metrics, that are easily accessible to the public or require paid subscriptions \citep{liu2024towards}.
As a result, it is challenging to objectively evaluate these methods due to their reliance on proprietary models or insufficient research evidence \citep{kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowertwo}.
Recognizing this resource limitation, our paper is structured into three main sections with distinct objectives:

\subsection{Reward Modeling} 
To foster more effective and efficient methods of AI-assisted scientific writing, we construct an open-source, large-scale benchmark with 50,000+ papers from \texttt{arXiv} called WAIWIG (\textbf{W}eb \textbf{A}gentic \textbf{I}nter-\textbf{W}riting \textbf{I}diasyncratic \textbf{G}eneration) (\cref{fig:overview} (a)). 
This benchmark has the potential to advance research on inter-active writing methods. 
To facilitate the training and evaluation of these methods, we introduce a benchmark-specific, state-of-the-art (SOTA) open-source reward model (\cref{fig:overview} (b)) trained with approximately 30,000 samples. 
Unlike common methods that either utilize human annotators or self-learning strategies \citep{lambert2024rewardbench}, our reward model, also trained on WAIWIG, is tailored to academic writing and is powered by both structured data and textual content. 
This approach not only optimizes the use of human resources but also preserves higher intellectual property (IP) levels (e.g., the authors can maintain their anonymity). 
Our benchmark and reward model are standard tools to measure the performance of different writing methods. 

\subsection{Agent-based Writing Assistant} 
Within the WAIWIG benchmark framework (\cref{fig:overview} (a)), we design an innovative interactive agent-based writing assistant method. 
This tool employs small, lightweight models instead of large language models (LLMs) to enable multi-round interactions with scientists for reviewing their writing (\cref{fig:overview} (c)). 
Our tool integrates Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning \citep{wei2022chain, pang2024iterative}, Self-Verification (SV) (a variant of Reflexion\footnote{\url{https://reflectionbook.io/}} \citep{shinn2023reflexion}, and self-learning strategies \citep{yang2024collaborative, zhang2024generative}, leading to a significant enhancement in the quality of generated reviews and paper generations (\cref{tab:main_result}). 
Our agent-based writing assistant method has the potential to improve the quality, efficiency, and scope of AI-assisted scientific writing.
To ensure user-friendly and high-quality results for our writing assistant method, we implemented a rule-based quality control and embedded a paper structure control process to guide the generation of high-quality reviews and papers. 
Our tool is open-sourced in user-friendly, Plug-and-Play format, allowing users to easily integrate and operate it for writing.

\subsection{User Study Evaluation by Scientists}
The effectiveness of existing AI technologies in academic writing is largely unknown due to the lack of quantitative data \citep{ai4science2023impact}. 
To address this gap, we conducted a large-scale user study to evaluate the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews conducted by our writing assistant tool (\cref{fig:overview} (d)). 
We invited experts in the field of artificial intelligence for science (AI4Science), including professors and researchers, as evaluators. 
The perceptual quality evaluation assesses the readability, engagement, and trustworthiness of AI-generated reviews, while the functional usefulness evaluation measured review quality and paper generation quality.
Our results show a significant perception quality improvement in 80\% of AI-generated reviews and a main increase rate of 63.3\% in the generation quality of AI-generated papers (\cref{tab:main_result}). 
Overall, the AI-generated reviews and papers are perceived as more trustworthy and useful by scientists when they participate in multi-round discussions to provide more detailed information and context. 
We also observe that scientists are willing to pay for the WAIWIG tool to further develop and improve its various features and functionalities (e.g., novel inter-AI scientific discussion method, AI paper co-authoring tool) to enhance user experience and further advance research.

\section{WAIWIG Benchmark}


\subsection{Dataset}

These papers and reviews are structured into consistent formats, facilitating various research directions.
For example, the common text format allows us to study standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) and generative model tasks \citep{bao2021predicting}, domain knowledge extraction \citep{nuijten2016prevalence}, and intent recognition \citep{wang2023scientific}.
Additionally, we provide \texttt{JSON} file formats for easier use in multi-agent settings \citep{huang2024mlagentbench} (e.g., setting up channels for text-based multi-agent communication), enabling researchers to easily develop AI agents for scientific writing.

Our benchmark includes 52,123 papers and 59,472 reviews, covering various domains such as Computer Science, Mathematics, Physics, and Economics. 
It also includes various disciplines (e.g., Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning). 
The paper analyzes the most popular domains in \texttt{arXiv}, including Computer Science, Mathematics, Physics, Economics, and so on. 
It provides an overview of domains, topics, and split sizes for tasks including classification, classification for in-the-wild text \citep{bao2021predicting}, extraction, intent recognition, sentiment analysis, and others \citep{langley2024integrated}.
Furthermore, the review analyzes the quality of reviews from a textual perspective, such as readability, readability vs. informativeness tradeoff, coercion measures, security measures, and logical correctness \citep{li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning}. 
It includes additional data from Reviewer GPT \citep{liu2023reviewergpt}, which is used to compare with other models and aid in identifying potential biases in paper and review generation.

\subsection{Data Generation}

The data generation process begins with the collection of papers and reviews from \texttt{arXiv} (except for data from Reviewer GPT). 
These documents are structured and cleaned to standardize their format. 
Subsequently, we calculate and analyze key textual characteristics for both papers and reviews, such as their length, complexity, and vocabulary diversity. 
This analysis helps us understand the nature of the text data in our benchmark. 
In this process, we also create review rankings, which are important references for reward models. 
Additionally, we inject statistical information from \texttt{arXiv} such as pages (one page for 4 pages of text), title, domain, and so on for in-depth learning. 
\subsubsection{Reward Model}

Following the method of RewardBench \citep{lambert2024rewardbench}, we train both a classification model and a regression model, enabling both classification and rating score evaluation.

\paragraph{Reward Generation:}
To accurately measure the quality of reviews and papers, we assign grades to each one on a scale of 1 to 5. 
This grading system is based on our analysis of paper and review quality, as well as statistical data from \texttt{arXiv}. 
During the training process, both positive (high-rated) and negative (low-rated) samples are used to enhance the model's ability to recognize high-quality content. 
We employ a multi-agent learning approach \citep{Hu2024AutomatedDO} in both the exploration and exploitation stages. The model then learns to balance learning (training with new samples) and exploration (training with sampled data from previously learned knowledge).

\paragraph{Reward Model Architecture:}
Our reward model follows the Radford \texttt{base} series architecture \citep{Hinton06}, specifically Radford\_Base\_Model\_V1\_1\_4\_k\_32\_w0\_1\_532\_5550\_80\_Instruct, which is open-sourced by Mistral AI \citep{jiang2023mistral}. 
The model has 4.7B parameters, with a hidden size of 4,096, 32 attention heads, and an intermediate size of 13,008.
The output of the reward model is a rating of 1-5 and a classification label indicating the sample is either positive (rating $\geq$ 4) or negative (rating $<$ 4).
To summarize, we train both a classification model (with binary classification) and a regression model on approximately 30,000 samples. 
The models converge after about 7 epochs, which takes roughly 20 minutes with 20 A100 GPUs. 
In the future, we will continue to improve the accuracy and coverage of the reward model and support for training on a larger scale (for example, 100 billion scale).
\paragraph{Quality Control:}
To ensure the quality of reviews and papers, we implement a rule-based quality control system that leverages the reward model. 
This system computes a rating score for each sample of reviews or papers by averaging multiple individual scores. 
If a paper sample scores low (rating $<$ 4), we will re-extract the paper and review from \texttt{arXiv} and re-analyse or exclude it to maintain the quality of the dataset. 
This ensures that the benchmark consistently meets high standards for review and paper quality.

\subsection{Agent-based Writing Assistant}

In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the agent-based writing assistant and its variants.

\subsubsection{Agent Architecture}

In our agent architecture, we leverage a Plug-and-Play communication strategy (e.g., OpenAI API protocol) and design two types of agents: \textbf{web agent} and \textbf{assistant agent}. 
They are designed to simulate reviewers and authors, engaging in multi-round reviews and discussions. 
Key features of the agent architecture include:

\paragraph{Web Agent:}
The \textbf{web agent} leverages data from \texttt{arxiv}, including papers, reviews, and their corresponding metadata (e.g., ratings, and etc.). 
Each web agent reads the papers and corresponding reviews with \texttt{``rating score''}. 
The web agents can provide feedback for the writing assistant and analyze the performance of the writing assistant. 
The web agents will be \textit{replaced} by human users in future real-world use.

\paragraph{Assistant:}
The \textbf{assistant agent} is dedicated to supporting users (e.g., writers) in reviewing scientific papers. 
The assistant agent accumulates web agents' papers and reviews, then summarizes and concludes the overall opinion about the paper and reviews from the web agents. 
Naturally, the assistant agent can collect ratings from the web agents as the context for decision-making. 
These functions will be implemented in user-friendly and Plug-and-Play format. 

In the future, we will deploy web agents on mobile devices and integrate them with real-world users to create a mobile app. 
Users (e.g., writers) can directly interact with the mobile app and access the functions.

\subsubsection{Agent-based Writing Assistant}
Based on the agent architecture, we design a variety of interative writing methods and their variants including:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Chain of Thought (CoT)}: 
    Following the DAgger \citep{hutter2001towards}, we allow the writing assistant with CoT evidence extracted from existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arXiv} (by GPT-4) to generate high-quality reviews.
    We then ask SOTA language models including GPT-4 \citep{achiam2023gpt} and Qwen2-13B-Chat \citep{qwen2.5} to rate and rank these reviews. 
    We use the average ranking score and rating score from the language models as the reward for the writing assistant with CoT. 
    We will use CoT method in multi-agent learning \citep{Hu2024AutomatedDO} to improve the writing assistant further.
    
    \item \textbf{Self-learning (self-learning):} 
    We simulate CoT (evidence) as reviews by writing assistants with existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arxiv} (by GPT-4). 
    The reviews are then rated or ranked by the reward model. 
    We use the average ranking scores and rating scores from the reward model as the reward for learning the writing assistant. 
    We will use the self-learning method in Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAC) \citep{lowe2017multi} to improve the writing assistant further.
    
    \item \textbf{Chain of Thought (CoT) + Self-learning (self-learning):} 
    We allow the writing assistant with CoT evidence and high-quality reviews to generate reviews. 
    The reviews are rated or ranked by the reward model. 
    We use the average ranking scores and rating scores from the reward model as the reward in multi-agent learning to improve the writing assistant further.
\end{itemize}

In total, four samples of each agent-based writing assistant method are collected for evaluating the perceptual quality in the user study.
To evaluate the functional usefulness, the writing assistant extracts tasks from existing reviews with GPT-4 (replacing CoT evidence) and completes tasks by the writing assistant with existing high-quality reviews in \texttt{arXiv}. The generation quality is measured by the accuracy, BLEU, or GPT2 PLM pretraining loss.

\subsubsection{Interactive Discussion App}
In addition, we design a user-friendly mobile app called ``Interactive Discussion'', which allows multi-round discussions between writers and LLM-based scientists (web agents) for quality control. 
It includes three main functions:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Invite Web Agents:} 
    The writer or app can automatically download web agents in pre-defined groups (defined by domains, topics, and etc) from cloud storage or user-defined web agents (from the upload file or online access). 
    \item \textbf{Privacy:} 
    The app password-protects the access to uploaded files by writers and encrypts the upload files and chat history (including upload files and chat history) in transit. 
    This feature can provide a higher level of intellectual property (IP) protection and allow authors to maintain their IP with confidence.
    \item \textbf{Mobile and Plug-and-Play:} 
    The app is designed to be easily used on the mobile, and also on desktop with less than 5 GPU (e.g., A100 GPUs). It can be easily integrated into workflows with simple Plug-and-Play interfaces and API calls.
\end{itemize}

In future versions of the app, we will integrate more features (e.g., AI co-authors) into the app and gather more user experience (e.g., ratings and reviews from users).



\section{User Study by Seasoned Scientists}


To measure the perceptual quality and functional usefulness
of AI-generated reviews by our writing assistant in comparison to other methods, we conducted a large-scale user study involving scientists experienced in the field of artificial intelligence for science (AI4Science), including professors and researchers, as evaluators.


\subsection{Objective}

Our user study has three main objectives to evaluate the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews and papers: 

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item \textbf{Perceptual Quality Assessment:} This part of the user study investigates whether scientists think the AI-generated reviews are useless, boring, and boring and difficult to read due to unfamiliarity with the content. Instead of measuring the actual quality of the reviews, this part focuses on the perceptual quality as felt by the scientists. It aims to evaluate the readability, engagement, and trustworthiness of AI-generated reviews.
    
    \item \textbf{Functional Usability:} This part of the user study assesses the functional usefulness of the AI-generated reviews in scientific writing. It measures how effectively the reviews help researchers in reviewing papers. The evaluation focuses on the reviews' usefulness in understanding and evaluating paper content. 
    \item \textbf{Paper Quality:} This part of the user study evaluates the quality of AI-generated papers compared to manually written papers. It measures how well these papers align with research articles on \texttt{arXiv}, including content, depth, and novelty. The evaluation aims to assess the potential of using AI-generated papers in real research reviews and to identify any gaps in their quality compared to human-crafted papers.
\end{itemize}
\subsection{Experimental Settings}

In this user study, we use GPT-4 generated reviews and papers as the base for comparison. 
Concretly, GPT-4 generates high-quality writing assistant reviews with CoT as evidence (4.88 ratings) and self-learning (4.74 ratings on average). 
GPT-4 writing assistant for paper generation (4.36 ratings on average). 
Human-written reviews have an average rating of 4.54, and research papers have an average rating of 4.64. 
We invited experts in the field of AI-assisted academic writing including professors and researchers in the AI4Science field (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), PhD students (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Peking University), PhD students (e.g., Chinese Academy Sciences, Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), MSc students (e.g., Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Jiaotong University), and so on, to participate in the user study. 
We invited and invited 36, including 11 AI4Science professors as evaluators in the perceptual quality assessment. 
We invited and invited 39, including 15 AI4Science professors as evaluators in the functional usability and paper quality assessments. 
The perceptual quality assessment and functional usability assessment are conducted through an online survey. 
The paper quality assessment is conducted through an online written test.

\subsection{Results}

\paragraph{Perceptual Quality:}
In the perceptual quality assessment, we surveyed 36 scientists, including 11 AI4Science professors, to evaluate the AI-generated reviews' readability, engagement, and trustworthiness. 
The results (\cref{tab:main_result}) showed that 3.95 ratings is the highest score on AI-generated review quality. 
Among 36 participants, 80\% of them believe the quality of AI-generated reviews is better than that of Reviewgpt method. 
Among 36 participants, 42\% of them believe the quality of AI-generated reviews is better than that of GPT-4 method. 
The results indicate that AI-generated reviews provided by our writing assistant are generally perceived as more trustworthy and useful than those generated by other methods used in the user study. This suggests that integrating CoT and self-learning approaches are effective in improving the quality of AI-generated reviews. 
We also conduct an anonymous interview with the scientists in the AI4Science field (e.g., Beijing University of Postgraduate Studies), and their main views are:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item Generally, the AI-generated reviews and papers are perceived as more trustworthy and useful by scientists when they participate in multi-round discussions to provide more detailed information and context.
    \item Scientists show a lot of interest in using AI to assist in writing. 
    They are willing to pay for the WAIWIG tool to further develop and improve the various features and functionalities (e.g., novel inter-AI scientific discussion method, AI paper co-authoring tool) to enhance user experience and further advance research.
    \item Most of the researchers believe that AI-generated paper summaries are useful and align with research articles on \texttt{arXiv}. 
    They showed a lot of interest  in using AI to co-author their papers. 
    \item The researchers and PhD students believe that the quality of AI paper writing is similar to that of the researchers at postdoctoral stations, and AI can help liberate the time of scientists to engage in deeper research topics, which can efficiently advance scientific progress.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Functional Usability:}
In the functional usability assessment, we surveyed 39 scientists, including 15 AI4Science professors, to assess the functional usefulness of the AI-generated reviews compared to human-written reviews. 
The results (\cref{tab:main_result}) showed that the AI-generated reviews provided by our writing assistant method achieved the highest perceptual quality score of 3.95. 
They achieve higher scores than GPT-4 and RF-GPT methods, which demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach. 
Functional usability scores and ratings show a main increase rate of 63.3\% and 22.3\% of the research papers respectively. 
This reflects the strong potential of the AI writing assistant to contribute effectively to scientific writing, significantly enhancing the research process efficiency.

\paragraph{Paper Quality:}
In the paper quality assessment, our writing assistant method demonstrated a 63.3\% main increase rate in accuracy and 0.21 GPT2 PLM pretraining loss main increase rate over GPT-4 method. 
It achieved the highest paper quality scores and ratings on all metrics, indicating that the AI papers produced by our method are of the best quality and usability. 
These results highlight the potential of our approaches in advancing AI-assisted paper writing.



\section{Related Work}


\subsection{AI-assisted Writing}
Large language models (LLMs) \citep{achiam2023gpt, reid2024gemini, qwen2.5, llama3herdmodels}, including ChatGPT, GPT-4, Gemini, Baichuan, have revolutionized writing with their exceptional language understanding and content generation capabilities. 
These technologies have significantly enhanced productivity and inspired new writing methods. 
Several platforms \citep{ai4science2023impact, langley2024integrated} \citep{wang2023scientific, kuzmin2024fp8quantizationpowertwo, zhu2024safetylock, zhu2024locking} have been developed to assist and improve the research process. 
They aim to streamline tasks like paper tracking, literature collection and analysis, experiment design, and automation. 
These platforms integrate with digital labs to centralize research data and assist in building experimental designs. 
We focus on directly assisting scientists in writing, optimizing the writing process from two perspectives: paper writing and paper reviewing. 

\subsubsection{Agent for Paper Writing:}
AI-assisted writing has seen a significant shift from rule-based expert systems to neural-based LLM methods \citep{wang2024autosurvey}. 
Rule-based expert systems, which rely on hard-coded rules and domain knowledge, have been surpassed by LLM-based methods that leverage vast training data and capabilities like in-context learning and language generation \citep{ai4science2023impact, wang2024loragalowrankadaptationgradient}. 
Early neural-based methods included zero-shot LLM-based and fine-tuning LLM-based \citep{liu2024towards}. 
These methods have evolved to include prompt-based methods like chain-of-thought and custom prompt-based methods \citep{achiam2023gpt}. 
Fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} and self-supervised learning have enhanced task-specific training for domain-specific writing. 

\subsubsection{Agent for Paper Reviewing:}
Peer review is a key part of the academic publishing process \citep{smith2006peer, boughton2018research}. 
Automation algorithms have the potential to improve review accuracy, reduce bias, and expand the pool of reviewers \citep{Bengio+chapter2007, Hinton06, NEURIPS2020_6b493230, NEURIPS2023_91f18a12}. 
Contributions like automated AI-assisted paper reviewing aim to aid researchers in writing peer reviews and increase the efficiency of the reviewing process \citep{robertson2023gpt4, li2024mlrcopilotautonomousmachinelearning, du2024llms}. 
Recently, researchers have begun to address concerns about the effectiveness and biases in existing AI-based reviewing systems \citep{hosseini2023fighting, zhang2022investigating}.

\subsection{Scientific Discovery}
Recent decades have seen a proliferation of research on the application of AI and machine learning within the scientific domain \citep{Bengio+chapter2007, Hinton06, lecun2015deep}. 
This work explores AI and machine learning applications across various scientific fields, including materials science \citep{merchant2023scaling}, chemistry \citep{pyzer2022accelerating}, biology \citep{hayes2024simulating}, and protein discovery \citep{jumper2021highly}. 
Researchers have tackled the generation of chemical \citep{buchanan1981dendral} and mathematical \citep{lenat1977automated, lenat1983eurisko, hueteropera2024mathematical} theories, and AI has accelerated the discovery of new knowledge \citep{hayes2024simulating}. 
The integration of AI has led to greater efficiency, novelty, and accuracy in scientific research, though its implications for creativity, authenticity, and disclosure of methods remain Marsh \citep{hayes2024simulating}. 
AI has transformed fields including materials discovery \citep{pyzer2022accelerating}, life sciences \citep{merchant2023scaling}, and protein \citep{jumper2021highly}. 
Recent developments, such as agent-driven automatic research \citep{lu2024ai}, survey generation \citep{wang2024autosurvey}, and hypothesis generation \citep{radensky2024scideator}, aim to streamline the research process, from data collection to the creation of surveys, hypotheses, and problem formulations \citep{wang2023scientific}.

\subsection{Scientific Agents}
Recent studies address NLP research tasks with LLM-based methods such as LLM-empowered literature review models, review generation, and automatic data curation \citep{liang2024can, hosseini2023fighting, tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext}. 
The application of LLM-based methods in peer review has improved accuracy, transparency, and exploration capabilities \citep{taniguchi2024collective}. 
Researchers have developed review agents emphasizing authenticity, fidelity, accuracy, and adaptation \citep{tan2024peerreviewmultiturnlongcontext}. 
Simultaneously, LLM-based methods have enhanced paper writing tasks such as concept clarification, literature summarization, target literature selection, and scientific writing \citep{wang2023scientific}. 
These methods help researchers formulate problems, review literature, and draft papers \citep{liu2024towards}. 
Researchers at OpenAI have employed SFT on LLMs across paper, idea, and experiment channels, focusing on writing assistance, paper summarization, and experimental design \citep{liu2023reviewergpt}. 
Other researchers have fine-tuned smaller models for scientific tasks such as literature collection, concept extraction, literature analysis, and summary extraction \citep{liu2023taxonia}. 
AI Scientist, an open  AI system, uses SFT strategies and to automate the entire research process from hypothesis to the publication of scientific articles \citep{lu2024ai}. 
The system's components include AI researchers, strategists, reviewers, code generators, and writers, suggesting that researchers could automate the writing process using specialized modules.

\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{User Study}
In the user study, there is an opportunity to incorporate a broader range of participants, including researchers from disciplines other than AI4Science and different research fields. 
This eclectic mix would yield a more comprehensive and diverse evaluation of AI-generated reviews and papers, ensuring a wider perspective and field of analysis. 
In the future, we will continue this user study and expand the number of participants to a few hundred researchers from hundreds of different research fields and disciplines, and also AI4Science researchers. 
This comprehensive approach promises a more accurate reflection of user perceptions and preferences, enhancing the overall quality of the evaluation.

\paragraph{Animal Study}
The results of the animal study are promising, showing that WAIWIG agents have good transferability across different domains and agents trained in one domain can be used to assist writing in other domains and fields (e.g., the agent trained in the computer science domain can be used to assist winter weather research). 
In the future, we will sample a larger amount of data in other fields and train a reward model to support more other domains, agents, and fields.


\section{Conclusion}


In this paper, we introduce WAIWIG, a novel solution to artificial intelligence-assisted scientific writing, with a focus on advancing the field through three key contributions.

First, we create a large-scale, open-source benchmark that features a diverse collection of scientific articles sourced from \texttt{arXiv} to foster advancements in AI-assisted academic writing and inter-results multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Second, we developed a groundbreaking interactive agent-based writing assistant tool and integrate it with the curated large-scale benchmark, enhancing the quality and efficiency of scientific writing processes.
Third, we have conducted a large-scale user study to measure the perceptual quality and functional usefulness of AI-generated reviews conducted by our writing assistant tool in comparison to other methods.
We will continue working with scientists to continuously improve WAIWIG for assisting in writing and conduct a broader user study (e.g., different AI-assisted scientific writing fields) to gather more user experience (e.g., ratings and reviews from users).


\section{Potential Impact}


We have implemented quality control mechanisms to protect the integrity and privacy of the research. 
These include deidentifying and anonymizing data during the review process, implementing strict review policies to ensure ethical practices, and restricting access to certain datasets. 
These measures will also help to promote ethical research practices among AI researchers and innovators.

motivation: The process of scientific discovery is inherently challenging due to its complex nature, characterized by uncertainty, inter-disciplinarity, and the need for evidence-based arguments. Despite the advancements in artificial intelligence, the process of scientific discovery through peer review remains critical, ensuring that findings are sound and reliable. Existing methods to automate peer review using large language models (LLMs) have shown limited success and unsupported hypotheses. For instance, ReviewGPT does not explicitly promote LLMs' attention to key words like 'evidence', and its output is often unsatisfactory. ReviewBot introduces a formalized context in the prompt but overlooks the necessity of complete reviews. MAVer, while performing well in some aspects, lacks robustness in maintaining completeness and accuracy. These limitations highlight the need for a more advanced and automated approach to peer review. This paper aims to address these challenges by proposing a novel framework that utilizes language agents to simulate and automate the peer review process, ultimately enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of scientific discovery.
idea: The paper introduces WUPReview, a framework that employs fine-tuning and automated LLM feedback to improve the quality of peer reviews. WUPReview fine-tunes LLMs to enhance their understanding of scientific papers, focusing on key concepts like 'evidence', and uses a multi-round review process where language agents provide feedback and iterative improvements. The framework achieves a 91% winrate against human reviews in related papers and a 72.5% winrate in an unseen setting, demonstrating its potential in automating scientific discovery.
title: WUPReview: A Quality-focused Writing-guided Peer Review System with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We propose \ours, a writing process-guided peer review system based on language agents for scientific discovery. \ours is designed to improve the writing quality of research papers, guided by a quality-focused prompt-engineered language agent in a multi-round format. To achieve this, we first finetune an LLM to comprehend the writing styles of a specific format and concept to facilitate the review. \ours then provides automated refinement and iterative learning based on writing feedback. It achieves state-of-the-art performance in various metrics, including an average 91\% winrate against human reviews in related papers. This demonstrates the potential of \ours in automating scientific discovery, signifying a significant advancement in the application of artificial intelligence to the process of peer review.

motivation: The field of AI-assisted scientific peer review has seen significant advancements, but existing solutions primarily address specific sub-tasks such as idea generation, body generation, and quality assurance. None have offered a comprehensive model capable of the full peer review of scientific manuscripts through the entire process. This gap is due to the inherent role-playing requirements of peer reviewing, which involve various expert abilities and must adhere to specific workflow rules. The full process of peer reviewing encompasses five main roles: expertise, cognitive judgment, consistency with review quality assessment criteria, adherence to work and duty ethics, and familiarity with manual operation. However, current methods often fail to integrate these aspects effectively. For instance, ReviewGPT and AutoReview provide references for LLM-assisted reviews but do not address the inherent role-playing requirements. RewardBench evaluates LLM-based rewards but does not provide a full process solution. This paper aims to address these challenges by introducing a novel AI-assisted reviewer LLM that integrates role-playing capabilities with a structured workflow, aiming to provide a comprehensive model for full scientific peer review.
idea: The paper presents Reviewer LLM, an AI-assisted reviewer LLM designed to perform full scientific manuscript peer review through role-playing and a multi-round iterative refinement approach. The LLM is guided by fine-tuned reward models, iterative preference optimization (IPO), and chain-of-though optimizations. The study assesses Reviewer LLM through three dimensions: general quality assessment, recommendation quality, and review quality. The results show that Reviewer LLM outperforms human reviews in general and quality assessment, outperforms Author-ASSIST-revised in recommendations, and performs competitively with Author-ASSIST and Author-ASSIST-revised in review quality, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of this approach.
title: Towards Full AI-assisted Peer Review: Scientific Peer Review Assisted by AI Reviewers with Review Quality Analysis
abstract: AI-assisted scientific-peer reviewing is groundbreaking and meaningful yet rarely explored. To address this challenge, we developed \method{}: an AI-assisted reviewer LLM that can perform full peer review of scientific manuscripts through role-playing and a multi-round iterative refinement approach. We fine-tuned reward models, applied iterative preference optimization, and chain-of-though optimizations to optimize \method{}. To assess its effectiveness and efficiency, we conducted a comprehensive quality analysis of reviews generated by human and LLM-assisted reviewers through three dimensions: \textit{general quality assessment}, \textit{recommendation quality}, and \textit{review quality}. Extensive results show that \method{} outperforms human reviews and OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo in general and quality assessment, outperforms Author-ASSIST-revised in recommendations, and performs competitively with Author-ASSIST and Author-ASSIST-revisd in review quality, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach.
